VANCOUVER FACILITIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I wish to present a motion on a question of urgent and pressing necessity. The urgency and necessity of consideration and action now flow from the calamitous and scandalous inadequacy of facilities and confusion surrounding the operation of the port of Vancouver by the National Harbours Board. The unprecedented volume of both exports and imports so vital to the survival of the Canadian economy has been seriously impeded by a lack of dock capacity, by delays of many months by the government in naming directors to the National Harbours Board, and in the constituting of the Port of Vancouver Authority, and other factors within control of government. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan):
That the whole question of the administration and facilities of the ports of Canada, the administration of the National Harbours Board and the direction thereof by the government, particularly the Minister of Transport and his officials, be now referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for examination and report, including recommendations to this House.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INTEGRATION OF MAIL TRANSPORTATION SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the Post Office Department intends to implement a major change in its transportation services in a number of urban centres across Canada.
The intent of the Post Office is to integrate urban mail transportation services in major areas of Canada in order to help stabilize mail transportation in these centres whose continued operation is essential to the maintenance of a national postal network.
The proposed integration means that the Post Office will undertake the intra-urban mail transportation previously carried out by private contractors.
In announcing this major change, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that among the major postal administrations of the world, Canada is the only country which does not now have integrated transportation services in its urban centres.
The decision to implement an integration of urban mail transportation services comes after a series of studies by the Post Office Department. As a result of these studies, integration was successfully undertaken in sections of Montreal and Vancouver as early as 1967.
As a further consideration, Mr. Speaker, in 1968 section 31 of the Post Office Act was revised. This revision provided that following the invitation to tender, no contract should be entered into for a term of more than five years. At that time the department knew it would eventually integrate all its major urban transportation services. The Vancouver and Montreal experiments of 1967 were undertaken to test the feasibility of this course of action.
In order to carry out integration of these services, the Post Office will require personnel, vehicles and support equipment. All those full-time contractors' employees who are working in functions related to postal work will be offered positions with the Post Office. The Post Office is conscious of its obligation to these men and is most desirous that they will elect to enter the Public Service. Many of these workers, after providing service to the Post Office for so many years, already regard the Post Office as their real employer. The Canadian public, too, has come to regard them as Post Office employees.
The unions representing these employees have been consulted and they are co-operating with the department in implementing this program.
As far as vehicles and equipment are conerned, the Post Office will offer to buy the material that the contractor now uses to provide his services.

November 23, 1971
Mail Transportation Services
Two criteria were used to define the centres that would qualify for inclusion in the program. Both criteria are based on mail volumes and are:
1.	Those centres which account for 1 per cent or more of the national total of originating first class mail, or
2.	Those centres which account for 10 per cent or more of the total of a postal region's originating volume.
These criteria define the cities and areas that are vital to the postal system in national terms. Not only are they important in their own right as major centres, but many of them are main in-transit or transfer points for the movement of mail originating elsewhere.
Application of the national and regional criteria result in the inclusion of the following metropolitan cities in the program:	Vancouver, Victoria, Edmonton, Calgary,
Regina, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, London, Metro Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, Kitchener-Waterloo, Ottawa-Hull, Metro Montreal, Quebec City, Saint John, New Brunswick, Moncton, Halifax-Dartmouth, St. John's Newfoundland. Of these 19 cities, four-Montreal, Quebec City, Windsor and part of Vancouver-are already wholly or partially integrated. The 15 new centres include satellite postal operations in urban communities adjacent to metropolitan areas. The total number of urban centres to be brought into the program, therefore, will be 42.
The integration program is planned to be completed by the end of 1972. Discussions with the contractors concerned regarding the dates of integration of individual services are starting immediately.
As the integration program is mainly aimed at the stabilization of key centres of the national mail network, it is not the intention of the Post Office to integrate those mail transportation services provided to rural or semi-rural areas, or between cities.
I believe that this move will help to bring a greater degree of stability to a most important element of Canada's mail system and as such constitutes a major step forward in the development of an increasingly reliable mail service.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INTEGRATION OF MAIL TRANSPORTATION SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of a series of announcements that have been made by the Post Office Department since 1968. I listened very carefully to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), and once again I find that this proposed change is being made in the interests of efficiency and better mail service in Canada. The minister was kind enough to supply me with a copy of his statement, and I note that the change is designed to stabilize mail transportation within the major centres of Canada.
It goes without saying that the sort of stability we want with respect to intracity mail transportation matters-I am sure the Postmaster General will agree with me-is not the sort of situation portrayed by the Lapalme drivers parading daily on Parliament Hill. I have followed the changes made by the Post Office Department in recent years, and the difficulty has been that with every change costs have gone up and services have gone down. The result is that the public are unhappy, the employees are

unhappy, and I am sure the Postmaster General is also very unhappy.
Those who listened to the noon broadcast of the CBC news today once again heard an expression of unhappiness and discontent from the public in the form of a protest by an advertising executive who is so unhappy about the postal service that he is going to take action against the department to recover the costs he has incurred in getting the sort of service he used to have before the announcement of assured mail delivery which the Postmaster General informed us was going to expedite the mails and which this gentleman, speaking through the CBC news, has referred to as a fraud and a disaster. I was also interested to note that he also urged the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) to investigate the Post Office Department to see if it is guilty of misleading advertising. Every time these changes are made there is a great spate of publicity and propaganda indicating an upward and onward trend whereas following the implementation of the changes we find that the quality of service spirals downward and only the costs of the service are onward and upward.
I think it is not a prejudiced viewpoint to express the opinion that every change announced by the Postmaster General and his predecessor, who was more of a disaster than the present incumbent of that post, has created confusion in postal services. This means that every change is not necessarily progress. I suggest to the Postmaster General that if he is really going to restore the confidence of the public in the postal service he must restore the morale of the postal employees. They make daily contact with the public and it is largely through the esprit de corps manifested by the postman on the walk, the postal employee at the wicket, the private contractor who in the past carried out the function that is now going to be handed over to direct postal employees, that the public's confidence in the Post Office Department is going to be restored. I was pleased to note on page two of the announcement that the Postmaster General emphasizes the fact that all full-time contractor employees engaged in functions related to postal work will be offered positions in the Post Office.
I think the hon. gentleman will agree that before the current labour difficulties which are harassing the postal service are resolved, before the morale of the employees is restored, before the confidence of the public is restored, there must be engendered in the postal employees-and there is now going to be a larger number directly involved-that spirit that used to be described in this poetic language: "Neither sleet, nor hail, nor rain, nor other vicissitude will deter them from their appointed task."

speechtext:
The proposal which is made is obviously a necessary one but whether it will be a good one will depend entirely on the way it is brought into effect. The experience we have had in the Post Office so far is that labour relations in that department have been a shambles for some years and that the Post Office has not yet got rid of the paternalism, indeed, the patronage, from which it has suffered for so many years.
The Postmaster General says that the department consulted the unions representing the employees of private contractors. May I say to him with all the kindness I can that an assurance like that does not reassure me at all. I should like to know exactly what kind of consultation took place, when it took place, whether the unions concerned were in fact given an opportunity to express their opinions as to how the proposal might be implemented, or whether the consultation in this case has been the same as in every other case, namely, that they were informed that something was going to be done. I emphasize that, Mr. Speaker, not out of any desire to be critical but out of a vivid memory of what happened in Montreal and out of the fact that we are still plagued with the results of incompetence and lack of simple human decency in the way in which the Lapalme situation in that city was handled. If better relations are not established, if the unions now concerned in this work having been given real consultation instead of phony consultation, then we may well have some difficulties in the future.
May I finally say to the Postmaster General that I was astonished, indeed, outraged this morning when I learned from officers of the Canadian Union of Postal Employees, a union that now represents some of the people involved in working for private contractors, that it was not even informed that this change was coming, let alone consulted, and that they are meeting with his deputy or someone in his department at 2.30 this afternoon when for the first time they will be told of this program that the minister has announced. That not only astounds me, Mr. Speaker, but makes me fearful about the way in which this thing is being handled, because not only is this union already in negotiation with the department or with the Treasury Board but it represents some of these people. Therefore, when the minister said that all the unions representing these people have been consulted, obviously he was not right. One of the unions, and perhaps the most important so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, was not even informed, let alone consulted. They are particularly worried about the matter because this announcement comes only weeks before negotiations are to begin in January between the Canadian Union of Postal Workers and the Post Office Department. They are concerned as to whom they will be negotiating for in this area and about the kind of confusion that may result in the negotiations.
In short, obviously the scheme announced is desirable, but we in our party will wait to see whether this Postmaster General will, unlike his predecessor, handle relations with the employees concerned in a human and decent way, in a modern labour relations way, and not in the
Mail Transportation Services
oldfashioned way in which his department so far has functioned. I hope he succeeds. If he does, we will be glad to congratulate him. However, if he carries on as his predecessor carried on, not only every member of the House but every Canadian will be sure to condemn him and his department for inefficient, incompetent and, indeed, inhuman relationships.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INTEGRATION OF MAIL TRANSPORTATION SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) has just announced that in the most important parts of the country, the department intends to integrate urban mail transportation services into the public service. He added that the measure would stabilize mail transportation.
If the new policy is implemented, I am convinced it will improve mail transportation services throughout Canada because they now present weaknesses. For instance, I noticed yesterday that the dailies from western provinces such as Alberta, and particularly those from Calgary, were not yet in the reading room of the House of Commons.
Mail from British Columbia often takes from 10 to 12 days to reach us in Ottawa. I hope the new policy of the Post Office Department will improve mail service by speeding it a little.
As a result of the new policy announced by the minister who tells us that he has consulted the unions interested in the transport of Canadian mail, I wonder like the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) if the minister did indeed meet with all the unions concerned.
I also wonder whether that new policy was brought about by the Lapalme boys who are still demonstrating on Parliament Hill.
They have not yet been integrated into the Civil Service because there is a conflict between the government and the CNTU. Has the minister met with CNTU officials to solve the problem of the Lapalme boys? The department should find gainful employment for those who will thus be dismissed from private enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, we all hope that the Postmaster General will come to an agreement with the representatives of the workers, and even with the former employees of G. Lapalme Inc. I would not want us, for instance, to attach greater importance to the CNTU than to the workers.
If the object of this new policy is to increase the standard of living, the security of the individual who works or will work for the Post Office Department, regardless of what union he belongs to, I welcome it. Indeed, I hope the government will adopt measures to favour the individual and not some of the Canadian unions. Let that be understood.
I hope this new policy will encourage greater respect for the human being rather than favour the abstract organization we see at work across Canada.
At any rate, I am satisfied that the Postmaster General is anxious to improve the postal service in Canada. He is also eager that the employees involved get all the necessary consideration from the Post Office Department so that they have gainful employment which will guarantee their security.
November 23, 1971

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, November 22, consideration in committee of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act-Mr. Benson-Mr. Laniel in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
In accordance with the statement of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council, as recorded at page 9777 of Hansard of November 22, 1971, the committee will now proceed to consideration of Sections 21, 25, 46 to 48 inclusive, 59, 64 to 66 inclusive, 87 and 124, all dealing with mining and petroleum.
On clause 1-section 21: Cost of borrowed money.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 21 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I have already set down some of the views I have with respect to the mining industry in the debate on the general provisions of Bill C-259. I have spoken of the harmful effects of the legislation on prospectors, who will virtually be put out of business. I have also spoken of the restrictions that are being imposed, not only by Bill C-259 but by other restrictive legislation before the House, and of the disastrous effect that these restrictions will have on the growth of this industry. I want to approach an analysis of those sections of the bill in a general way, from the point of view of what is desirable in this country, and how we should be treating this industry, indeed any industry.
However, I intend to confine my remarks to the mining industry. Others on this side of the chamber will be speaking on the measure as it affects coal and timber resources, and yet others will be speaking of the manner in which the oil and gas industries will be affected. As I say, I want to confine my remarks generally to the hardrock mining industry. I want to approach the subject by suggesting at the outset to the government that what it should be doing, instead of applying suffocating restrictions, is providing incentives for the industrial growth of the country, and in particular of the mining industry.
Under existing legislation, tax treatment of the mining industry is contained essentially in the income tax regulations, and it now appears that this concept is to be carried forward in Bill C-259. This is one of the major criticisms that the industry has of this manner of dealing with its taxation. There is no way that the industry, dependant essentially upon large amounts of risk capital, can plan sufficiently far ahead-in some cases it has to plan five to seven years ahead-with any accuracy if the rules of the game are going to be changed half way through the planning period, or indeed month by month as is possible if this whole operation is going to be covered by regulations made by Governor in Council.
I make specific reference to section 65 of the bill, which is found on page 155, where the following is set forth between lines 22 and 27:
Income Tax Act
There may be deducted in computing a taxpayer's income for a taxation year such amount as an allowance in respect of an oil or gas well, mineral resource or timber limit, if any, as is allowed to the taxpayer by regulation.
There is the power to tax. Another criticism can be made with respect to that kind of regulation, namely, that the power to tax is the power of Parliament, and that is where it should reside. But this section of the bill would give that power to the Governor in Council. It seems to me that that is the ultimate in the weakening of the power of this place, passing the power to tax over to the Governor in Council.
In order to achieve a new tax treatment quite similar to the old one, namely, that tax treatment of the mining industry is to be contained in subsequently prescribed regulations, the government has seen fit to issue occasionally its general intentions. These intentions have been released in the form of vague, poorly phrased proposed regulations. Furthermore, it may be shown that the spirit and intent of certain of these proposed regulations seem to change with each new issue of them.
Specific reference is made here to proposals made by the Minister of Finance in August, 1970, on the subject of eligible expenditures to earn depletion. At that time it was proposed to expand these eligible expenditures to include, first, the cost of new facilities located in Canada to process mineral ores to the prime metal stage and, second, certain expenditures in connection with a major expansion of an existing Canadian mine.
On July 6 of this year the Department of Finance issued further proposed regulations to apply to the mining and petroleum industries. Included in these new regulations were a series of proposals that, as they now stand, are not only ambiguous but contradictory to those of August, 1970. This is another example of the changes proposed for the act introduced by the Minister of Finance, followed by a second batch of proposed changes and a third batch of proposed changes. The same thing is happening with the proposed regulations that are being issued, all of which is causing extreme difficulty, if not making it impossible for the mining industry to make any plans at all based on the so-called proposed regulations.
Such changing attitudes by the government in its proposed tax regulations have contributed in no small measure to an unsettled business climate in Canada's mining community. Specific reference is made here to a submission by Noranda Mines Ltd. to the Standing Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. I am sorry I do not have the page number, but the committee report reads:
Noranda has undertaken a $120 million program of expansion in the province of Quebec, relying on our understanding of the Minister of Finance's announcement of August, 1970 that all of these expenditures would be eligible to earn depletion. Based on the spirit and intent of that announcement, there is no conceivable reason why all of these expenditures should not earn depletion. Now we find that $40 million of these expenditures will not qualify.
This submission by Noranda Mines continues:
We were led to believe that the announcement of August, 1970 was specifically designed to encourage developments of this type. Had we not believed that all of the expenditures involved would have earned depletion, the project would probably not have proceeded, at least on its present scale. Changes in the intent of the

Income Tax Act
August, 1970 announcement at this stage are clearly inequitable, to put it mildly.
Not only are the changing attitudes of government toward certain sectors of the economy inequitable, but it is becoming more apparent that the government is also becoming increasingly restrictive. Specific reference is made here to the restrictive attitude of the government toward the natural resource industry in general, and toward the mining industry in particular. Subject to further clarification it now appears that the proposed tax regulations will have the effect of withdrawing exemptions for prospectors, and I have mentioned that; replacing the three-year tax-free period for new mines after 1973 by accelerated depreciation rates on some assets of that new mine; earning a depletion allowance of $1 for every $3 of certain expenditures. This elimination of the three-year tax exemption period for new mines, particularly in the northern regions of the country, is going to have an absolutely devastating effect, not only on the exploration and search for new mineral deposits but also on the bringing into production of new mines. In addition, the regulations will discontinue shareholders' depletion allowances. Obviously, such measures are restrictive and if implemented, could seriously hinder the orderly expansion of one of our most important industries, the mining industry.
At a time when the government is showing more manifestations of its restrictive policies, as in the field of foreign ownership, serious consideration must be given to the effect such restrictive policies will have on the ability of the individual Canadian to invest and participate in the growth of our domestic natural resources. Specific reference is made here to the existence of drilling funds. I have mentioned this on a prior occasion in debate as an example of how the United States policy toward investment funds is actually hindering the development of Canadian resources, because Canadian investment dollars find it a good deal more attractive to find their way into the United States and come back here by way of investment capital rather than being put directly into investments at home.
American tax laws favour the use of essentially private capital for these drilling funds in a risk-taking venture, such as oil or gas exploration, by granting certain incentives to individuals willing to take such risks. These drilling funds were discussed in some detail by me in this House on October 18 of this year. How much better it would be to gain more control over our own resources by attracting more Canadian investment dollars in our resource development industries, and by providing incentives at home at least equivalent to those being provided by the United States government to their investors, than to take restrictive measures in the hope that those measures will be the be-all and end-all of repatriating our resource industries.
The point to be made at this time is that rather than adopt a restrictive policy toward ownership and development of resources in this country, much more consideration must be given to policies that further individual initiative and reduce state interference and control to a minimum. Quite obviously, one means of achieving such a policy of individual initiative is to establish tax incentives comparable to those in the United States that encourage an individual to invest more private risk capital in Cana-
[Mr. Nielsen.J
da's natural resources. The influx of large amounts of such domestic capital into Canada's resource industries will provide an opportunity that will allow concerned Canadians to express their feelings about foreign control of these resources in a more positive manner than could ever be achieved by the main recommendation of the Gray report, that is, the setting up some sort of screening process to direct the inflow of investment capital in this country.
The principles of tax incentives as against tax restrictions can be applied to a wide field. It has already been indicated that tax incentives for individuals to invest in Canada's natural resources are a suitable means of providing an avenue for greater individual participation in the growth and development of our economy. One further area that relates to tax incentives and the mining industry must be mentioned. This area is the field of environmental control and pollution abatement by the mining industry.
The latest Department of Finance news release on tax reform proposals for the mining industry referred to certain allowable assets eligible for accelerated depletion under regulations not yet published. Although the list of eligible expenditures included buildings, mining machinery, social capital and such items, no mention was made of the cost of pollution abatement equipment necessary to meet industry emission standards. Surely, this is one incentive that the government should be holding out to this industry in order to meet the increasing threat of pollution.
In summary, it may be said that although the principle of tax treatment by regulations prescribed subsequent to enactment of Bill C-259 allows some flexibility, particular caution must be exercised at this time that these proposed new regulations remain consistent and in the best interest of the country. If indeed the government intends to proceed in this fashion on the matter of writing the requirements into acts so that the mining industry knows where it stands and we must have regulations, then I submit these must be consistent and in the best interests of Canada. It has already been shown that since the first public appearance of the proposed new tax regulations both the spirit and intent of certain of these regulations have changed. How many more regulations are there to come and how will these differ from those presently proposed?
Of equal or perhaps greater importance is to assess the new tax proposals and to evaluate their potential contribution to the socio-economic interests of Canada. It is apparent that the present government intentions are to further restrict development and ownership at a time when serious consideration must be given to an incentive tax program. To this end, it is now proposed that rather than adopt restrictive measures, tax incentives be made available to achieve the following objectives. We must first strengthen the domestic mining industry to the extent that it is able to compete with international concerns. It is not so important to look at any tax advantages the domestic mining industry may have relative to other domestic industries, but to see what disadvantages the domestic industry has relative to international concerns. If the government does not think that is important, let us
November 23, 1971

analyse for a moment the burgeoning development of mineral industries in countries like Australia.
Second, we must provide a climate that encourages individual initiative and risk capital investment in domestic natural resources. A comparable scheme to the American drilling funds must be actively considered in the broader context of Canada's mining industry. Third, we must provide tax incentives for environmentally conscious industry. Serious consideration should be given to including costs of pollution abatement equipment in the list of expenditures eligible for accelerated depreciation.
Others on this side will deal with the specifics of these and other proposals, with specific parts of the resource industries of the country and the effect that this tax reform bill will have on them. In a very general way, I have tried to point out to the government that what we require for the development of this country is an incentive approach rather than a restrictive approach.

Mr. Chairman, there has been much discussion in this country about incentives for mining industries. At the moment, it appears that all the representations made to the government about removing the great advantages that have been given to the resource industries of Canada have met with little success. The government has ducked its responsibilities. It has backed away from its original position, and has backed away from recommendations in the Carter commission report to the effect that the resource industries should be treated in relatively the same way as our other industries are treated, and that special concessions given to those resource industries over the years have been inequitable and unfair. I submit that those advantages have been positively damaging to the economic future of this country. We have paid out money to destroy our own economy. We have given tax concessions and received little in return.
I realize that the provinces of this country which almost totally depend on resource development will find the proposition I am putting before Your Honour difficult to accept. I can imagine hon. members saying, "It is fine for the hon. member for Waterloo to say that. He comes from an industrialized area of Canada. It is fine for him to be an advocate of the manufacturing industries, but where does his position leave, say, British Columbia, Alberta or the Yukon? I admit that there are difficulties connected with the position I am adopting.
On the other hand, I think we should discuss these matters frankly. Quite often debates in this House on the merits of resource industries as against those of manufacturing industries take on the appearance of a civil war. Often those debates transcend party lines, support for one or other of the propositions being put forward being divided along provincial lines rather than along party lines. That is understandable. However, the position we face is serious. Unless we can resolve this problem and stop seeing ourselves as a country of fractious segments, there will not be a country called Canada. We shall not be able to develop effective trade policies, and we shall not be able to develop an effective tax system. We must find some way to resolve this particular difficulty.
Income Tax Act
I hope hon. members listening to me will give me the benefit of the doubt when I say that I am speaking not only for Ontario and for the highly industrialized parts of the country, but I am speaking for all Canada. I am very much concerned about what is taking place. Canada is being excluded from virtually every major market for manufactured goods in the world. The same applies in many cases to our agricultural products. The United Kingdom, which has long been a traditional market for us, will adopt many of the restrictive measures of the European Economic Community. Many difficulties are in store there for our grain farmers. The United States is becoming increasingly protectionist. I feel that this United States sentiment will not disappear quickly. Notwithstanding the possible removal of the 10 per cent surcharge in the near future, the protectionist sentiment of the United States will increase. That country is looking inward. I do not think that the United States has embarked on these measures merely because the Prime Minister of Canada invited the premier of Russia and president of Yugoslavia to this country. That is what some hon. members have suggested, and I do not believe it. These United States moves were on the books long before these visits took place.
Surely, hon. members are not suggesting that Canada should not try to maintain relations with other countries of the world and that we should not make an effort to resolve many international difficulties that we, a member of the world community, face. When we look at Japan, what do we see? There is a market in Japan for our raw materials and some of our foodstuffs, but there is no market for our manufactured goods. When we look at the American position, what do we see? It has become clear, I think, that the United States wants from Canada raw materials and energy supplies, and no more than that. I am sure that some people in Alberta will applaud that. They will say, "This is great for Alberta." No doubt some people in British Columbia say, "We are shipping coal to Japan, and that is great for British Columbia." There is only one problem connected with this, Mr. Chairman. If we pursue a policy of exporting only raw materials and of encouraging, through our tax system, this kind of export, we shall in the end have opted out of nationhood. There will be no future for us as a country and we might as well realize it.
We could argue that in terms of coal, iron ore and oil, we have at the moment a position of considerable advantage so far as the United States is concerned. As I say, we could argue that and say that simply by increasing exports from primary industries we would increase the per capita income of Canadians. There is only one big "if" in all this. If we do that, we will not be able to maintain a population of 22 million people. We will have to cut back on our population sharply and export our people, as Ireland did many years ago. There is no way that we can sustain the present population in Canada and accommodate in employment the number of people presently in the labour force if, in future, we emphasize the export of our raw materials. The raw material industries are capital intensive industries. They are not large employers of labour. According to figures I have seen, the raw material industries employ about 150,000 people. They provide about 150,000 jobs out of a total of more than 3,500,000

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
jobs in the country as a whole. That shows how serious the problem is. We must decide whether we are to be exporters of raw materials or the manufacturers of goods and providers of services.
When we were starting out as a new country and did not have our present population or infrastructure, we had to depend on what was traditionally called a fish and fur economy. What else could we do but export our resources, resources such as timber and minerals? Today, however, the choices open to us are different. Actually, we do not have a choice if we wish to maintain our population. The idea of depopulating Canada is-well, it is unthinkable. It is not acceptable and I do not know how it could be done. That is to say, I do not know how one could say to the young people of this country, "There is no future for you here; all we are doing is exporting raw materials. That is what we are encouraging through our tax system. You had better find yourself another country in which to live." I say this with the utmost seriousness. At the same time I say to those hon. members who come from resource rich provinces, "I understand your position; yet you must also understand the awful dilemma facing this country."
I would never suggest for a moment that we should cut back on the present rate of production in the mineral industry. That is not what I am suggesting, nor is any member of my party, I think, suggesting that. We are suggesting that we should look to the future and not encourage the export of raw materials from Canada either directly or indirectly through the tax system, as at present. We should instead find a way of saying to the resource provinces "We will meet your grievances. We understand your needs. We understand that this will have some effect on your future development, therefore, we will have an overall industrial policy for Canada that will compensate you for some of the development that may be forgone by you. Where that is not possible, we will at least have a provision for sharing the rewards of industry and resource development equally on a per capita basis to stop this constant civil war, this schizophrenia that exists within the boundaries of this country and which will ultimately destroy this country unless we find a way of resolving it."
I realize that some of what I say sounds a little dramatic. I do not wish to sound dramatic. This is something about which I feel very strongly and something which has been too long neglected. The kind of debate we are having today has often been turned into one of the east versus the west, as though we were enemies and not part of the same community and commonwealth. Therefore, in my remarks today I propose to examine some of the mythology-perhaps I should not say "mythology" because some members may take exception to that. I wish to examine some of the things-we have always believed about the resource industry and its value to Canada as a whole. I want to see to what extent that concept really bears examination and to what extent it really has validity for a country that has a choice of becoming a manufacturing nation or continuing to be what is often called the greatest underdeveloped country in the world.

I wish to quote some words of Mr. Ralph Nader who is visiting Canada. This statement is reported in the Ottawa Citizen for Saturday, November 20, and is a direct quote:
"As long as you are an extractive super-colony, and as long as decisions affecting U.S. investment in Canada swirl around U.S. considerations, the Canadian interest will come out second best."
Those remarks were made by an American. He said other things along the same line. A few weeks ago another American visited Canada on a mission for a group of businessmen in the United States. He made the following remark which was reported in the November 17 edition of the Globe and Mail:
"If I were a Canadian-which I sometimes wish I were-I would be less concerned over the temporary surcharge and more concerned over your exports of raw materials to the United States. It is not fair for Americans to use up Canadian resources faster than Canadians use their own."
This statement in the Globe and Mail is attributed to Mr. C. F. Hachmeister. We have a lot of resources in this country. I am not trying to denigrate for a moment the scope of our resources. However, regardless of that scope, they are still finite. There is a limit. In a number of years, we could remove them all. We could go further afield into more expensive and more difficult extractive areas, but what happens when the resources give out? What are we left with? What does this country do for an encore when it has exhausted its resources? We must not forget that as vast as the resources of Canada are, the insatiable appetite of Japan and the United States will consume them at such a clip as to leave us aghast.
In the early days, we thought that pollution was no problem. We said "Look at our beautiful rivers and waterways. Look how fast they flow to the oceans and lakes. What are a few bits of dirt?" We learned to regret that position. The smokestack in the city was a sign of progress and satisfaction. We are now in danger of destroying ourselves because of the close proximity of those smokestacks. The dye, slag and chemicals pouring into our rivers were considered signs of progress. We were wrong. We were wrong when we cut down certain areas of our forests and did not replace these areas with tree cover. Who thought it would be a mistake to take trees out of a country like Canada that had so many trees? As rich in resources as we appear to be, and as infinite as these resources may appear at the moment, they have a limit. If we do not husband them carefully and decide on their allocation, we will not have any resources. We will not survive, except perhaps as some northern slum of the United States.
An interesting item appeared in the October 29 edition of the Globe and Mail. It is an example of the kettle calling the pot black. The item deals with the Canadian Petroleum Association and reads:
-the mining industry will carry a 21 per cent collective tax burden while the petroleum industry will shoulder a levy of 36 per cent after 1976 when the legislation comes into force.
This is absolutely shocking. Imagine the mining industry getting away with paying only a 21 per cent tax while the dear old petroleum industry has to pay 36 per cent. It is shocking to both sides. At the moment, some estimates indicate that the oil industry is only paying a 6 per cent tax on its profits and the mining industry is only paying 13 per cent. It can be seen how seriously we are disadvantag-
November 23, 1971

ing those industries and how unfair we are vis-a-vis the mining industry versus the oil industry. Nevertheless, I wonder how much sympathy we should allow ourselves to have when we consider that every other industry in Canada is paying the full tax, around 50 per cent, and in many instances providing far more employment than either the mining or oil industry.
It is not fair to those industries that are paying their full share of taxes to continue that practice, while the resource industries receive special privileges. Any kind of special privilege in society, whether it be a special privilege for one individual in contrast to another or one industry in comparison to another, arouses resentment. It does not increase the feeling of co-operation in society or the sense of belonging to the same society. There is a cause for grievance and division. So it should be. We like to think of ourselves as a fair society and a fair country. However, as long as we have tax laws on the books that treat one group of investors more favourably, for no good reason, than another group of investors, it is going to be difficult to maintain any kind of pride in the degree of equity that exists in Canada.
Another argument that is often used is that because other countries grant concessions to mining industries, most of the capital that goes into the mining industry, or for that matter the oil industry, is specific capital. I grant that the people in the mining business are in the mining business. They are not likely to go into the foam rubber business. If you do not provide the same kind of opportunities and the same kind of concessions in Canada they might get in Nigeria or Chile they will go elsewhere in the world, although they may have some reason to regret a decision to go to Chile as they may if they decided to develop mines in Ireland. Of course, these companies are helping to bring about this kind of talk. The distinguished hon. member for Yukon made that argument in his remarks a few minutes ago.
Unless we are prepared to give them the same benefits here in Canada they will go elsewhere, but this presupposes a number of things; that resources in Canada are equivalent to resources elsewhere, and therefore we have to give exactly the same concessions. In many cases our resources are richer and by giving the same concessions we are augmenting the profits of the companies. If they do not get what they want in the way of decent taxes and concessions they may not act in the national interest, perhaps not deliberately but because the activity of the company does not conform with our long-term outlook and planning. That being the case, why would we want them anyway?
There is considerable evidence to indicate that because we have been so generous in our tax system in respect of resource development, we have attracted much more money into these industries than even the market system would justify. The kind of argument advanced by the hon. member a moment ago cannot be justified in a free enterprise system or even in a social democratic system. A social democrat is more inclined to believe in planning and looking ahead to the future. He believes the people should have a greater say in determining their own destiny instead of leaving this to impersonal market forces.

The social democrat is appalled at the idea that concessions should be given which frustrate the long-term objectives of the nation.

My concluding point is that in no philosophical system could we really justify a distortion of our tax system in order to bring more mining activity to Canada. After all, the people working on the Barber commission were not social democrats. Those people believe in a free enterprise system and their argument is that by providing these exaggerated benefits we have hurt ourselves and distorted the proper functioning of our economic system.
I hope to have an opportunity to say a few words later on in this debate. Let me conclude with those arguments and by expressing my appreciation to hon. members for the extended time they have permitted me.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to say that my remarks will be confined to section 65. I should like to say a few words with specific emphasis on the timber industry and coal mining. At the outset, I should like to comment briefly on the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo. I found much in his very fine address with which I can agree. I should like to say, however, that with regard to the natural resource industries it is a fair comment that perhaps one should remember when one is tampering with industries of this magnitude, and accusing them of having special privileges, at least by reference, that it is upon this very important sector of the economy that we must depend to receive the impetus this country needs for its continued progress and development. Certainly, academics cannot provide it nor, with respect, can civil servants or politicians. There is a question as to whether those in the service industries can provide the necessary expertise to generate wealth and create prosperity. When one considers this country has always been primarily dependent on the success of these primary industries, I think perhaps in some cases at least, there is a case to be made for making sure that if they do not have any special privileges, these resource industries are handled with great care.
As far as the timber industry is concerned, I do not intend to say very much but, for the record, I think in

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
considering the effects of section 65 on the timber industry the government has already recognized to some extent that other natural resource industries such as mining, oil and gas, require certain earned depletion allowances and expenses. If they made those concessions, as rightly they should, on a comparable basis for the pulp and paper industry this would have an equal effect. It would then be equitable and logical to consider giving this industry a system of earned depletion comparable to some of the depletion allowances which exist in respect of other natural resource industries.
For example, I think a depreciation allowance on antipollution equipment necessary to meet new emission standards would be worth while. It would make good sense, as well as good ecological practice, for pulp companies to improve their facilities with the very latest equipment. I think significant mill expansions at this time might be questioned. However, in so far as market conditions permit, there should be some concessions made there. As anyone knows who has worked on certain logging projects, there are some primitive conditions. Among the expenditures eligible for allowances would be social costs relating to the installation of roads, camps and other facilities for the employees.
It is with the coal mining industry that my thoughts are this afternoon. This is a very important industry, not only to Canada but to my province and to my constituency. It would appear that the national coal industry is fairly healthy. It may even be said to be in a "turnabout" position, and it might even be said it will expand rapidly during this decade. In 1969, for example, domestic coal production from all provinces was something over 10 million tons, and at the present time it is greater than that. In 1970 it was 16.6 million tons, up about 55 per cent. I see the parliamentary secretary smiling. Perhaps he doubts the efficacy of our research department, but according to the information I have this year's production will be over 20 million tons.
As far as the eastern coal industry is concerned, we do not have the benefits of long-term contracts with Japanese purchasers. As everyone knows, our coal industry is in serious trouble. This is because the government in its wisdom has decided to permit United States coal, from states like Pennsylvania and Kentucky, to come into the largest domestic market in this country, namely Ontario. This is possible now because, as a result of the Kennedy Round, the duty is off this coal. At the same time the government has seen fit to drop, to a large extent if not in fact entirely, the subsidy payments which permit transportation costs to be kept within reasonable limits in order that the maritime coal industry can compete in Ontario. As an example, the latest figures show that the production of coal in the Maritimes is down sharply. It would appear this is a result of a deliberate federal policy to stabilize maritime coal production at what could be said to be the subsistence level.
For example, New Brunswick coal production declined by 43 per cent in 1970. In Nova Scotia, coal production declined by 19 per cent as compared with 1969, from 2,621,000 tons to 2,122,000 tons. In the west, British Columbia's production increased by 280 per cent; the
[Mr. MacKay.J
increase amounted to 132 per cent in Alberta, and in Saskatchewan it was 89 per cent. There are certainly reasons for this. With all deference to western coal, it is of a much lower quality than the coal of Nova Scotia and eastern Canada generally. It is sub-bituminous. In fact, the so-called red coal of Saskatchewan is not much better than peat in terms of thermal efficiency. By contrast, Nova Scotian coal is almost up to the anthracite level in qualify and is in great demand when it is available. The drastic decline in our coal production came about, as I understand it, because of the removal of the subvention payment made by the federal government in respect of transportation costs.
Returning to the specific difficulties which the mining industry will encounter and relating them to section 65, it seems to me the key to this situation is that we cannot treat coal in the same way as other minerals are treated. For example, when we talk about exploration costs we must realize that most of the areas in Canada where coal exists have been known for many years, and there is really not much by way of exploration costs that the mines can write off. This is not, of course, the situation in which the nickel and copper mining industries find themselves. Again, the provisions with respect to earned depletion allowances are impracticable for maritime coal producers, simply because, as I understand it, in order to qualify they are obliged to increase their production, or increase their capacity to produce. But under present conditions it is hardly likely, as statistics show, that they will be able to do so. In fact, instead of production increasing by the necessary 25 per cent in order to qualify, in all likelihood production will decline still further unless drastic steps are taken.
At the present time coal producers enjoy certain advantages in the same way as do gold producers. Under the regulations now in force, gold producers benefit from a depletion rate amounting to 40 per cent of production profits or $4 an ounce, whichever is greater. The comparable figure with regard to coal is 10 cents a ton. Under the new tax proposals, as I understand them, effective January 1, 1972 these special rates will be replaced by earned depletion allowances identical to those available to other producers of minerals. I suggest this is a wrong approach because it is unrealistic as far as coal is concerned. It would seem to me that the intention of the federal government toward coal mining in Nova Scotia is to allow the smaller mines to operate without assistance until they are forced to shut down. I would point out that the unemployment resulting from such a course would affect about 5,000 miners at least, not to mention their families.
I have recent correspondence from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources concerning the McBean coal mine in Thorburn. From this correspondence it is clearly evident that the government has no interest in modernizing this mine or taking constructive steps to increase its productivity by starting a new working level. In fact, it appears that the government is content merely to phase this mine out. This is a serious matter. Where there used to be literally thousands of miners working in Pictou County, for example, there are now only a few hundred, and when the McBean Colliery is closed, as now it appears certain to be, and the Drummond Mine in
November 23, 1971

Westville, the only other existing mine, ceases production, there will not be one place in Pictou County where coal is obtained, though millions of tons are available. A day will come, Mr. Chairman, when Canada will need the coal which is available in the East River Valley of Pictou County, as it will need the coal which is available in the rest of Nova Scotia. It will then be a case of starting from scratch, working with untrained personnel, very likely under emergency conditions.
One of the major provincial problems facing the operators of coalfields, at least in Nova Scotia, is that though the reserves are abundant, mining techniques are antiquated. In the west, on the other hand, coal is being produced by using the most modern machinery in conjunction with open pit mining. Leaving aside the question of the ecological damage which is done by strip mining, productivity and efficiency are certainly greater than can be expected from underground mining, even though, as I say, the quality of the coal produced in the west is not as good. Unless the government realizes that the mining industry does require special attention, particularly in Nova Scotia, we shall lose this industry completely. This may well result in another Glace Bay dilemma such as arises when one supports a marginal operation without attempting to improve it.
At a time when Canada's domestic market is using increasing quantities of imported coal, some initiative must be shown by the government so as to de-emphasize dependence on countries abroad and encourage domestic production and the development of mines, for the enrichment of the nation as a whole. I do not wish to get into a discussion about the merits of what Devco is doing in Cape Breton. It is not my field. However, it seems to me that the operation has not been a resounding success and that unless more attention is paid to the real needs of the coal industry conditions will soon be so bad that we might as well forget about it in eastern Canada. In western Canada there have at least been interesting concepts, such as the unit train. I suppose this development has been the result of a co-ordinated effort between provincial and federal government departments. I know of no such concepts having been introduced in eastern Canada, although one might think from the superior quality of coal in eastern Canada that a scheme of this kind would be particularly worth implementing.
In conclusion, it appears to me that coal, as I said before, should not be treated as just another mineral. It has special problems arising from its location, the difficulty of obtaining trained labour and the cost of transporting it to market, not to mention the effect of foreign competition, mostly from the United States. Any stable industrial economy needs an industrial base. Coal will be essential in the future if we are to make the best use of our primary resources. If we are to have cheap hydro-power available in Nova Scotia, coal will still be needed to help operate thermal generating plants. Coal is required in connection with our steel industry in eastern Canada.
The federal government should make immediate efforts to modernize our mines so that they can ultimately become viable. If we do not single out the coal mining industry as requiring some help, particularly in certain regions, we shall lose the industry, though the time will come when the demand for coal will justify the moneys
Income Tax Act
which would, could and should be spent at this point, quite apart from the benefits in employment and resulting social benefits. You will never find a better group of men than the coalminers. They work hard. They risk their lives and all they want is a chance to earn an honest living and produce benefits for this country. So far, they have done so with notable success. It should be a shame to lose this vital part of our economic life through unwillingness to make concessions to this industry, particularly in Nova Scotia.

My hon. friend from Waterloo was unduly sensitive, it appeared to me, because he happens to represent a constituency in a manufacturing area in a part of the country which members from the far west sometimes refer to as the wicked east. As a member who spent all his life in the two westernmost provinces of Canada, who spent at least ten years of his life in a mining community and who has developing mines in his own constituency, I thought it might be useful if I participated for a few minutes in this debate to indicate my complete support for the approach to this whole matter as presented by the hon. member for Waterloo. Anyone who has lived in the atmosphere of a mining town and anyone who understands how completely dependent on a mining economy a particular area is-and the Yukon territory is a particular example-readily understands the concern of an hon. member such as the hon. member for Yukon, and indeed all of the members who have a high level of activity in their part of the country for the income tax law as it relates to that industry.
I should like to make clear, however, that it is a matter of regret to me that in this bill the government has rejected the approach suggested by the Carter commission. The Carter commission, as I recall its recommendations in summary, suggested, in thinking of the long-term situation in this country and of the future in particular, as well as its wealth in the form of non-renewable resources, that we should consider the timing and degree of our exploration and exploitation rather than have that exploration and exploitation left to the whims and fancies of the people actually engaged in the mining industry, or to the short term world market conditions which might prevail in respect of the salability of any particular metal at any given time. As the hon. member for Waterloo suggested, I feel it is important that we think in the longer term. Some of us from time to time have had an opportunity to travel within the boundaries of our great neighbour to the south. We have seen rather vivid examples of what has resulted within the boundaries of that country because of the traditional method of exploitation of non-renewable resources. Some of us suggest that while we still have time in Canada we should begin to think about the whole question of the manner in which these precious substances are drawn from the ground and our approach to that operation.
The lure of wealth, of course, has been at the root of the whole philosophy of mining as it has developed on this continent, stemming I suppose primarily so far as the whole western part of the continent is concerned, from the days of the great gold rushes. At that time men from all corners of the globe, some of the keenest, most adven-

turous, strong-minded and able bodied men, were drawn to the search for a precious metal. As a result of this situation, there emerged a whole pattern of attitudes and law. This, I believe, has been carried forward to this day and is fostered by the application of the kind of income tax laws we have had and will continue to have if the proposals in this bill pass in their present form.
We are all well aware of the fact that the mining industry, its associations and organizations, continually over the years have bombarded us with argumentation concerning the necessity for the special spurs that are needed to enable them to go out and find new mines. I suggest that even from the most practical point of view that argumentation becomes less valid as time goes on, partly because of the development of new technology, partly because the approach to the development of a new mine becomes increasingly a matter of scientific appraisal of the natural resources and their potential. As a result, when a decision is made to commit money for the development of a mine there is much more likelehood that the mine will, in fact, bring returns to the investors. I am speaking now about the serious type of mining, the type of mining that is carried on to draw wealth from the ground rather than the type of mining in which promoters are more interested in mining the more gullible members of the general public through the stock exchanges of the country.
I have a very basic disquiet about the way in which we are moving in this whole process. I feel this is something which requires a considered approach at the national level. Unless and until a new philosophy is enunciated in Parliament which would change our approach to tax laws, I believe it is virtually impossible for any particular area of the country to do anything but go along with the process of developing resources from a purely local point of view, even though that development may result in rather limited benefits. There is the example of a large mining corporation in my constituency which is just getting into production. In fact in the next month I believe they expect the first shipment of ore to leave the mine. This is a tremendous mining enterprise. The concentrators are designed to mill something like 33,000 tons of ore a day. With the already established reserves, there is a life expectancy for that mine of 25 years at that rate of mining. In the particular area in which it is located it will have a real impact upon the viability of the community. The particular community affected will probably double in size. Many of the amenities which can be had only in a community of reasonable size will result because this mine is coming into production.
As the member representing that area I certainly have not objected to the development of that particular mine in that particular location. It would be foolish for me to do so. It would be silly of me to suggest that this mine not be developed at that particular place when I know the general policy of the country is that such mines are to be developed wherever any particular mining company might decide it has the opportunity to do so. The fact remains that 25 years is not a very long time in the history of a country. The children of the people who will be working that mine will be reaching the point at which they will be presumably looking for productive work at about the time when the projected life of the mine expires.

This, of course, raises the kind of question that was raised by the hon. member for Waterloo, namely, what happens to the children of the current generation of miners at that mine? At the end of 25 years there will be a big hole in the ground and, under the current mining laws of the province of B.C., that kind of open mining operation will have to be completed in such a way that there will be at least some degree of restoration of the landscape. One proposal was that there be a new lake there, about half a mile wide and two or more miles long, that it be landscaped around the edge, and that a new recreation area be created. As it happens, on Vancouver Island there are a number of lakes already in existence. Of course, the same is true of many parts of Canada. Recreation areas are very nice, but even though one may be able to enjoy an inexpensive holiday in a recreation area of that kind, it is rather necessary that there be an economic base for the people who may want to use the recreation facilities from time to time. So the ore from that hole goes across the Pacific Ocean, the profits from the operation go across the border to the south, and in 25 years we will have a nice new lake in Canada. In the meantime, of course, incomes will have been provided for 400 or 500 people for 25 years. I suppose that this is not something to be sneezed at.
Those of us who live in the midst of this sort of thing have perhaps more cause to be concerned about it than have members who live in manufacturing centres, such as the hon. member for Waterloo. In the national interest we may or may not need the development and export of the ore from that particular mine at this time. But the result of the approach we are taking in our income tax law is to continue to encourage this helter-skelter, haphazard development of the extractive industries. This type of development I suggest-and I would like to emphasize this point because I do not think the hon. member for Waterloo made this quite clear in his speech when he spoke about resource industries-is in an entirely different category from that of renewable resources, whether that relates to products from the farms or the products of the forest. This latter type of activity will go on without any special or direct kind of encouragement such as, for example, has been provided for the extractive industries like the mining and petroleum industries.
All we are saying-and, as I understand, all that Mr. Carter said in his report-is that these extractive industries should be treated for income tax purposes on the same basis as all other industrial enterprises. If it was deemed to be in the national interest to accelerate the extraction of petroleum, of copper or of iron ore at any given time, we should do it directly above the table so that we know how much it is costing us. In this way we could tell whether this kind of expenditure was or was not in the national interest. As matters stand, the only way we can really come to grips with this matter is to discuss it indirectly when the Income Tax Act is opened up from time to time. I suggest that this is not the best way to approach this matter. I suggest that despite the kind of briefs we sometimes get-and they certainly come from organizations in my province, and the B.C.-Yukon Chamber of Mines makes the position clear to us from time to time-I am convinced that if these special provisions were to be
November 23, 1971

abolished it would not mean the end of the mining industry in Canada.
I am convinced that where there is a viable market for a mining commodity, that commodity will be produced because we know we have the natural resources to enable us to do so. Let the market be the yardstick as to whether or not we are going to have an increase in copper exports, just as it is in connection with the development of the pulp and paper industry in this country. If we find that the economic situation in that particular field is in a state of decline, if there is tangible evidence that it is necessary to accelerate the exploration for new sources of this kind of raw material, then let this Parliament decide that it is in the national interest to do it at a particular time and let Parliament appropriate the money for it to be done.
Hear, hear!

This, among other things, would bring a new rationale into the kind of thinking which prevails in the mining industry in this country. It would put an end to the everlasting beseeching and begging for more and more special concessions with which we are assailed by the mining interests today, and have been yesterday and the day before that. They would know that they could produce the minerals that were needed. They would know that if there was a real need, and it was in the national interest to open up new resources in new areas or to start more intensive exploration in already known mineral zones, they could present a straightforward case to the government, and that Parliament would be prepared to give it the kind of consideration it deserved. But as long as we continue this basic approach that is still being carried forward in this so-called tax reform law we will be besieged, and so will the Minister of Finance, for a little more and a little more. Frankly, I am very disappointed that the Minister of Finance and the government were not able to see the logic of the position that was put before the people of Canada and this parliament by the Royal Commission on Taxation.

The subject matter that is before the House today in this long continuing debate on Bill C-259 will, I am sure, have a sympathetic ear from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance who has been guiding the debate for most of its period in the House. Recently he was very disturbed in this House at the impact of the latest decision by the National Energy Board with respect to the curtailment of the export of oil and gas resources, and of gas in particular. I do not think it is necessary to belabour the point to convince the hon. gentleman that what is contemplated in the sections of this bill with respect to the resource industry in terms of tax reform is not in the best interests of that industry.
This afternoon I would like to point out that the sections of the bill which we are debating have the same basic weakness that we found in other parts of the bill. I think the assessment of this debate given in editorial comment by the Financial Times of November 22 is worth quoting to underscore the basic objection that members of the Official Opposition have raised to most of the sections of the bill. Certainly it applies to the sections covering the
Income Tax Act
resource development industry. The editorial reads in part:
In one way, Mr. Benson has a point. It really does not matter whether the MPs debate every clause of the bill. As delegates to the Canadian Tax Foundation conference sadly noted, the MPs are completely out of their depth in trying to debate or to understand the bill.
After several months of intensive effort, the most expert of the tax experts are only slightly less baffled than they were at the beginning.
The attitude of the Tax Foundation members . . .is one of fatalism and resignation. The tax changes are coming. Let them come. Somehow, we will muddle through.
The immediate result will be something akin to chaos. As it stands, the bill is a no man's land of ambiguities, obfuscations, and ill-defined intentions, entirely surrounded by uncertainty. It is going to take months and years of working experience to find out how the new system actually works, and what inequities it embodies.
I do not want to be too specific with reference to the bill, but I do want to spend a few moments pointing out to the government that obviously it is not aware of what it is doing to certain important segments of Canada's resource industry in the reforms contemplated by the bill. As I have also already indicated, the protests by the parliamentary secretary with reference to the petroleum industry are indicative that he is in sympathy with this viewpoint.
I want to discuss the impact that the bill will have on the continuing development of the Canadian north. The Canadian north includes, in particular, the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. It also includes the northern parts of the prairie provinces, of Ontario and Quebec, all of which form part of the Great Canadian Shield. The immediate effect of this bill will be to slow down the encouraging development that has been taking place in this whole area.
Even at this stage of anticipation when the shadow of implementation is hovering over the business community, when the threat of implementation becomes more real with each passing day, there is a hesitancy, and uncertainty in the market, all of which is reflected in the daily stock market reports. If the government proceeds to implement the bill in its present terms the impact on the north will be devastating. I make this point because the minister in charge of northern development has already revealed the thinking of the government on these matters through his action on Bill C-187 which was designed to bring about certain reforms, as he called them, in mineral development in the Yukon Territory.
The hon. member for Yukon, and other members on this side of the House who have been closely associated with northern development, took a strong stand against Bill C-187, with the result that the minister made a statement recently in the Yukon saying he will not be proceeding with the bill. He realizes he did not consult closely enough on it, and was not fully aware of the serious impact it would have on the development of minerals in the Yukon. Bill C-187 now lies in a state of limbo. In the light of the minister's comments, I imagine that it will remain there, or that if it re-appears it will be in greatly amended form along the lines recommended by spokesmen for the Official Opposition.

In this regard, I do not understand the attitude of members to my left concerning the impact that this bill will have on northern development. Recently the leader of the NDP said that the best solution for northern minerals was to freeze development and keep them in reserve. I have listened to the two spokesmen for that party who have spoken in this debate thus far, and while they did not go to quite that extent, the implication is that we should preserve, reserve and conserve non-renewable resources of the north for the benefit of future generations. Imagine what would happen if that were applied in the case of Thompson, Manitoba, which is represented by the former minister of highways of the province of Manitoba. Resource development by the International Nickel Company of Canada at Thompson has had a tremendous impact on the whole economy of Manitoba.
When I was minister of northern affairs, we used to have a slogan that I think is apropos at this juncture of our discussion. It went something like this, "Woe unto them who sit on their frozen assets." This is the policy that NDP spokesmen have been recommending this afternoon, and it is not only the NDP group who have made this statement. The government party has been what might be termed "Johnnies come lately" in the whole process of northern development. This can be illustrated by the reservations they had with respect to development of the Pine Point railway. This made possible the development of the lead-zinc mine at Pine Point and has largely been the basis of the great upsurge in resource development in the Great Slave lake area of the Northwest Territories. Yellowknife, the capital of the Northwest Territories, has become a modern metropolis through the impact of this one resource development. It would never have taken place had not the government of the hon. member for Prince Albert taken the risk which has always been typical of great development on the Canadian frontier, a risk taken over strong protestations of the then Liberal opposition, against the completion of the railway into the Pine Point community.
The same applies to oil exploration in the Canadian north. It was a small group of domestic minors-and I might add that is m-i-n-o-r-s as opposed to the foreign majors in the oil industry-who in 1960-61 gathered together sufficient capital to make it possible for Canadians to carry out the first oil exploration in the high Arctic at Winter Harbour on Melville Island in 1961. That was entirely a Canadian effort and is one of the great epics in Canadian resource and frontier development. This group was headed by Dome Petroleum under the leadership of Jack Gallagher, a Canadian active in the oil industry in Calgary who I am sure the parliamentary secretary knows intimately, and made possible by the vision and skill and pioneering spirit of another Calgarian, a comparatively young man named Peter Bawden who took in his drilling crew and drilled the initial well. I think the hon. parliamentary secretary will have good reason to become more familiar with Mr. Bawden as we move forward into the inevitable confrontation of democratic politics in the forthcoming election.
Nothing should be done to discourage this type of initiative, Mr. Chairman, and this is precisely the point made

by the hon. member for the Yukon. He wants incentives for Canadian participation in resource development to be expanded so that by getting more Canadians involved in the process we can repatriate ownership of our resource industry by positive means rather than the negative means of a screening process or some such measure. It was because the Canadian government of 1957-63 introduced regulations which gave some preference to Canadian exploration companies in operations in the high Arctic that we got that first pioneering oil venture. It was a very simple process. If a discovery was made the regulations ensured that Canadians had a chance to participate and to manage the enterprise.
Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary is thoroughly conversant with these matters and is just as concerned as hon. members on this side of the House about their harmful effect on resource development in Canada, so why does he not take the necessary initiative and amend the act? We have had hundreds of amendments already. The tax reform bill could be amended in such a way that it would encourage rather than discourage Canadian participation in the development of our northern resources in particular but our resources in all parts of Canada.
The hon. member for Galt went to great pains to point out that he was not speaking against the best interests of the western provinces-
He was not?
-with reference to the policy that he was enunciating. As I listened I was persuaded that Shakespeare had some relevancy here-"Thou dost protest too much"-
