speechtext:
He is the
member for Waterloo.
Waterloo-that is very appropriate. He was protesting too much because he went on to enunciate precisely the thesis he was repudiating.
You did not understand.

I hope the hon. member for Broadview will listen carefully, because obviously he does not understand either. He was enunciating the thesis that the so-called underdeveloped parts of Canada, the parts that are underpopulated and lack political impact in Ottawa because of that very fact, are being governed through Ottawa as if they were a colony of Ontario or Quebec. This is exactly the thesis propounded by the hon. member for Waterloo this afternoon. He even quoted that great American defender of the consumer, Ralph Nader. I am surprised that someone from his party would quote an American source because of their attitude toward our friends to the south, but Mr. Nader was quoted by the hon. member for Waterloo as saying-
Capital is from Waterloo.

-that Canada must not become the extractive colony of the United States. I would paraphrase that statement and say that the west and the north must not become extractive colonies of Ontario and Quebec.
November 23, 1971
That is what we are now. That is the problem. That is what we are trying to get away from.

That is the thesis that my friend from Waterloo was supporting. He also made a great deal of the fact that we are exporting most of our resources to the United States. I should like to point out to him that recently Japan has become a great market for the minerals of the Yukon territory. Were it not for the opening of this market in the early part of the sixties there would be no new Imperial Mine operating just outside Whitehorse, nor would there be the Anvil Mine which has been of great benefit to the Yukon Territory and has given employment to the Indian population by bringing the mineral from the mine to the railhead and trans-shipping it across to the open port and on to Japan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member. I must do so to advise him and the committee that his time has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may carry on if there is unanimous consent of the committee. Is there such consent?
Agreed.

Thank you for your courtesy, Mr. Chairman. I shall be very brief because I was just coming to a conclusion. We are concerned about what will happen to the Canadian resource industry when these resources have become exhausted. By the same token, Mr. Chairman-and the hon. member for Waterloo made much about this point-we are part of a world economy and of a world market. We must consider our international responsibilities. What will happen to Japan and its teeming millions if these resources are not available to the people of Japan? The hon. member was contradictory in his argument in that sense, in one breath preaching international brotherhood and in the other supporting the thesis that we must sit on our frozen resources until such time as we can use them for the maximum benefit of Canada exclusively.
Frozen assets?
I mentioned frozen resources. I have already made that point.
Is that the Salvation Army position? Shame.
I think that is a very good position for someone in that category to espouse; namely, that we should take seriously our responsibilities for brotherhood internationally as well as domestically.
Who said anything about frozen assets?
At least the hon. member was not being hypocritical.

Mr. Chairman, I say, now that these interjections have concluded, that I will leave this in the hands of the parliamentary secretary. He is fully conversant
Income Tax Act
with the subject. I trust he will take the necessary action to bring about equity and fair treatment for all parts of Canada, and that not only the central part of Canada will be so treated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Before recognizing the hon. member for Winnipeg North it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the Committee that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-Pensions-Old age security-Inquiry as to increase and lowering of eligible age; the hon. member for St. John's East-Regional Economic Expansion-Re-evaluation of policies in light of criticisms; the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway-Health-Family planning conference-Request for publicity campaign because of increase in illegitimate births.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon we heard a number of speeches by hon. members of the official opposition. The hon. member for Yukon spoke, as did the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. They were critical of the government's income tax bill, arguing that it will reduce or eliminate incentives which have been given in the past to the mining, oil and gas industries and that this will lead to a cutback in the development of those industries with consequent, deleterious effects for this country. The proposals in this tax reform bill affecting the mining, oil and gas industries do not in any real way do what members of the Official Opposition have charged. Actually, if there is one thing that is obvious, it is that these proposals continue the special tax concessions which in the last 25 years have been available to the mining and petroleum industries. These concessions were unjustified because the industries in question are, for the most part, foreign owned and capital intensive. They make use of a relatively small amount of labour. By asking for further concessions for these industries the Conservative party, in my mind, is betraying the real interests of the Canadian people. It seemed to me that the Conservative opposition wanted the government to make further concessions in this area. It has proposed that present concessions be continued.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris chided my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo. Although the hon. member for Waterloo had said that he did not want to see any conflict between our provinces, between the west and the east, his position, according to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, was essential pro-Ontario, a position which is inimical to the western provinces. I say to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris that, in adopting our position, we do so in the full knowledge of what we are doing. We are adopting the same position which the NDP government of Manitoba has adopted since being elected. Let me put on record, for the benefit of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, what the Minister of Finance of the province of Manitoba said in his budget speech on April 30, 1970. Talking about the white paper which this government had produced on tax reform, the white paper which, in a watered down version, is being implemented in the tax proposals before this committee, that Minister of Finance said:
Our main objection is that-contrary to the Carter Commission recommendations-the federal proposals are more concerned to

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
tax according to how money is earned rather than according to how much. This is contrary to "ability to pay" as a basis for taxation-
The proposals do not meaningfully redistribute income beyond the present structure. The biggest saving for a low-income person-$127 for a married man with two children and $4,000 a year. But if you were to earn over $50,000-there are actually provisions for reduction in tax. At $100,000 the reduction is $5,423-
Then the minister went on to say this about depletion allowances:
Depletion allowances and other resource industry incentives, etc., are still going to operate-these may well be wrong in principle-whatever the basis for computing them.
Then, he went on to say:
we-
Meaning the government of Manitoba,
-support the objective of making resource development in Canada more responsive to the particular needs of Canadian communities and citizens. This is not a passing comment. We seek tax proposals aimed to achieve greater responsibility to the community for enterprise deriving its main profits from the resources which belong to the people. The first major resource taxation concept to be questioned is that involved in depletion allowances. Why, for example, should only the private investor be compensated for depletion of resources and not the people and communities to whom the resources belong? Far greater concern should be given to the workers and communities who come to depend on the resource industries for their opportunities. It is they who will be the real losers through the depletion of natural resources. If firms continue to receive depletion allowances in any form, it is essential that such compensation be shared with workers and dependent communities.
I ask the hon. member for Brandon-Souris to remember who took the losses when the uranium mines at Elliot Lake closed down because there was no longer a market for uranium. It was not the companies, which had earlier written off their investment'. It was the workers who purchased homes at Elliot Lake. It was the government of Canada which, through Central Mortgage and Housing, had invested money in homes and it was the provincial government of Ontario which had built schools, roads and provided all the other services. The industry got off scot-free; the people paid through the nose. That is what the hon. member for Brandon-Souris wants to continue and to extend.
Shame.

We are not alone in our position on this matter. Before the present Minister of Finance ever became a cabinet minister he made some useful and interesting speeches in the House. I wish he would take part of an evening off to read some of the speeches he made while he was still a leading member of the opposition. I am talking about 1962, the year of which this afternoon's question period reminded me. It had that kind of spirit. I wish to quote two paragraphs from a speech which the present Minister of Finance made on November 9, 1962. He dealt with the policy of the then Conservative government as it affected the oil and gas companies. He said:
I can think of no other industry (oil and gas) in Canada in this favourable position.
I would think the next thing to consider is, who is going to benefit from these tax concessions contained in resolutions 6 to 10? Foreign control and ownership of this industry has been
increasing and this legislation, I submit, will do nothing to discourage foreign ownership and encourage Canadian ownership.
He was right.

In the same speech, he said:
We must, Mr. Chairman, find ways-and the next Liberal government will find ways-of returning the control of our natural wealth to Canadians while, at the same time, assuring foreign investors that they will be fairly treated by our government.
That speech could have been made by the hon. member for Waterloo. In fact, it has been made by him. The only difference is that when the present Minister of Finance moved from this side of the chamber to the other, he forgot everything he said before he became a member of the government. He immediately proceeded to continue the policies which had been implemented, not by the Conservative government which he helped to replace, but by former Liberal governments in 1947, 1948 and 1949.
To show that the position we are taking is not based purely on political partisanship, I wish to quote briefly from a couple of editorials which appeared in a newspaper which is not far removed from the Liberal party and its policies. This editorial, entitled "Oil men don't need tax gifts from Canada", appeared in the March 1, 1967 edition of the Toronto Star. I quote:
The commission-
That is the Carter commission.
-proposes to take away two cosy privileges enjoyed by these industries at the expense of the ordinary taxpayer-depletion allowances and the three-year tax exemption for new mines.-
The three-year tax exemption applies also, to mines. A mining company enjoys an exemption for the first three years on income earned from a mine newly brought into production.-
The special favors enjoyed by the two industries are extremely expensive. In 1964, it is estimated, they cost the federal treasury more than $150 million. This is about the equivalent of the government's combined spending in 1965-66 on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, and grants to universities.
Does this government propose to change that situation through this legislation? Not really. They changed the format of the concessions, but the concessions remain essentially the same.
I wish to quote from an editorial which appeared in the December 11, 1967, edition of the Toronto Star. It is entitled "Mines should pay fair tax share". I quote:
How can Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp justify his decision to dig new tax revenue out of the ordinary wage earner while continuing to provide special tax privileges to big business-notably the mining industry?
The Carter Royal Commission on. Taxation found that mining, along with the insurance and petroleum industries, was a potentially rich source of tax revenue that had long been enjoying unnecessary exemptions.-
The Carter Commission considered these exemptions unjustifiable. It recommended that the depletion allowances be eliminated immediately, and that the other privileges be phased out over a period of five years.
That seems to be squarely in line with what the Minister of Finance said in 1962 before he became the Minister of Finance. However, we have had no action by the government. Without a doubt, the most important speech made on taxation in recent years, and I believe in giving credit where credit is due, was the speech made by the hon. member for Duvernay. This is the speech which led to his

November 23, 1971

resignation. He did not just put on the record a theoretical argument. This is the same argument I am trying to make, but he did it much better than I.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why don't you just file it at this time instead of reading it again?

I suppose the reason the parliamentary secretary makes that stupid interjection whenever I quote from this speech is that he is embarrassed. When I make this kind of speech, I can be written off as a radical, a socialist and a person who never had to meet a payroll. All those things are true. However, when the hon. member for Duvernay makes that speech, he speaks as a professor of economics, a very successful businessman, the former president of the Montreal Stock Exchange, a former and one of the most effective ministers of revenue that any government in the province of Quebec ever had. The only difficulties the hon. member for Duvernay ever had were those which followed the terrible mistake he made when he decided to enter federal politics as a Liberal. From that time until he quit the cabinet, he made mistakes. The reason the parliamentary secretary always makes that idiotic interjection when I quote from this speech is that it embarrasses him. He knows that a lot of people who are still afraid and still worry about the New Democratic Party, will pay attention to an argument put forward by a man with the stature of the hon. member for Duvernay.
I remind the parliamentary secretary that when the member for Duvernay made that speech to the 300 academic, government, business and labour economists attending the meeting of the Canadian Economics Association, he was greeted with a standing ovation which the newspaper people who reported the proceedings said had never happened in the history of that organization. It may be that the hon. member for Duvernay was wrong, and that his argument could be shot full of holes. If this is so, I would like someone who knows a little more about economics than the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, and that is not very difficult, to reply to that speech. I am sure the Canadian Economics Association would be more than happy to invite the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance to their next annual meeting. While they may not be economists, they can get the assistance of the best economic advisors in Canada. They can get some help in writing their speeches.
I am sure the Canadian Economics Association would be happy to have one of those exalted gentlemen appear before them and rebut the speech made by the hon. member for Duvernay. That has not been done here or anywhere else in this country. The reason is that essentially the government has no answer. The best defence then is silence, except, of course, for the stupid interjections by the parliamentary secretary. The tables produced by the hon. member for Duvernay in his speech were taken from government reports. If they are wrong, I am sure the officials will quickly pass a note to the hon. member for Calgary South telling him they are incorrect. They go to the heart of the question we are discussing today.
In his speech, the hon. member for Duvernay used the table which is entitled "A Comparison of Book Profit Before Taxes and Taxable Income by Selected Indus-
Income Tax Act
tries". It covers the years 1965 to 1968, the latter being the last year for which figures are available. The table is arranged in three columns showing, respectively, the type of industry concerned, the taxable income received by that industry and the percentage of profits which were really taxed. For example, the retail trade earned book profits of $1,620 million. Its taxable income was $1,445 million. It paid tax, therefore, on 90 per cent of its profits. The wholesale trade earned profits of $2,066 million Taxable income amounted to $1,802 million. It paid taxes on 87 per cent of its taxable income. The construction industry earned book profits of $993 million, on $643 million of which it paid taxes, that is to say, on 65 per cent. The manufacturing industry showed profits of $12,745 million and paid taxes on $8,052 million; in other words, on 63 per cent of its profits.
Now, let us consider the industries we are discussing today. The metal mining industry showed profits of $1,707 million. Its taxable income was $222 million. In other words, it paid taxes on 13 per cent of its profits.
Shame.

The mineral fuel industry showed book profits of $795 million and paid taxes on $45 million, or 5.7 per cent of its book profits. Other mining enterprises showed profits of $374 million and paid taxes on $120 million, that is, at a rate of 32 per cent.
Members of the official opposition have been telling us this afternoon that these industries should continue to receive the concessions they have so far enjoyed. Indeed, they argue they should be given even greater concessions. Mr. Chairman, I do not care whether the government of Canada or the government of any of the provinces is a Liberal government or a Conservative government or a Social Credit government or an NDP government, it would still be obliged to collect taxes to meet the cost of the services it provides to its citizens. This is a simple matter. If one industry or another does not pay its fair share of the taxes, then other industries will be called upon to pay more than their fair share. When the hon. member for Yukon says we should continue to make concessions provided to the metal mines, which pay tax on only 13 per cent of their profits, or to the mineral fuels industry which pays tax on only 5.7 per cent of its profits, he is telling us, in effect, that the taxes which the construction industry, the manufacturing industry and the retail trade must pay ought to be increased, or that the personal income tax of those who live in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, and, indeed, the Yukon, must be increased to pay the taxes which those industries were permitted to escape paying. This may suit the hon. member for Yukon, Mr. Chairman, but it does not suit the members of the New Democratic Party. What he is suggesting is that we continue a system of taxing the poor to benefit the rich. He is advocating socialism for the rich, capitalism for the poor. That certainly does not suit me or members of my party.
I wish there were time in which to continue to put on record in detail the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Duvernay in his speech. I shall end by stressing once again the major points he raised. We can adopt a system of taxation which is mutual, which treats all industry equally, which collects the same rate of tax from every

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
business, allows the same concession and opportunities to write off depreciation and other expenses or we can establish a system which, because we wish to achieve certain objectives, favours one type of industry as against another. The point which the hon. member made so effectively was that in a country such as Canada, where the rate of unemployment is the highest in the western world, a country where unemployment has run at a seasonally adjusted rate of more than 6 per cent in every month for the last 17 months, we should surely be encouraging those industries which employ people.
Incentives.
Precisely. Incentives for industries which employ people. And those are the manufacturing industries.
What about the ripple effect?

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I did not hear any hon. member say no. It has been the practice during this debate to permit members to continue speaking if they wish to do so.
I thought it was one of his own hon. friends.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon has raised a point of order. The Chair asked whether there was unanimous consent. With respect, it is not for the hon. member to hear. It is for the Chair to hear and I can tell the hon. member I heard the word "No" quite distinctly. Thus, under the rules, I cannot permit the hon. member to continue.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact I am following the hon. member I want to make it clear that I did not say "No." I will have difficulty using up my allotted time.
I agree with the editorial referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. Very few Members of Parliament are really qualified to discuss this tax measure. Most hon. members are out of their depth when they attempt to discuss this 51-pound bill. I doubt if any other country in the civilized world has ever put forward a measure which weighs so much or was so complicated. I want to deal with it very superficially; I am not going into detail because I feel if I did so I would not know what I was talking about, as suggested in the editorial. The parliamentary secretary must be given credit for doing an excellent job. At least he pretends he knows what is going on and looks as if he knows. There is an award given in Hollywood for which I have no doubt the hon. member will be nominated next year. I believe it is called the Emmy award.
(Mr. Orlikow.]
For all practical purposes the majority of mining activity in the province of Newfoundland is located in my constituency of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. I use the federal name rather than the federal-provincial nomenclature. I refer to it as Newfoundland rather than the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. Federally it is the province of Newfoundland, which includes Labrador. We have in my riding the iron ore operations at Buchans which has been going on for several decades, providing a decent living for several thousand people. Close by we have the mining operation at Gullbridge, the mining operation in the Green Bay area, the tremendous Iron Ore Company of Canada operation and Wabush Mines in Labrador west.
The Iron Ore Company of Canada is going ahead with a big development. Present expansion plans at Labrador city, which is the location of the Iron Ore Company's operations, will double the present capacity of about 15 million tons. This will amount to 16 million tons of pellets, 10 million tons of concentrates and 5 million tons of raw ore.
Three or four miles away we have Wabush Mines Limited. In February of this year the company put the damper on an expansion plan amounting to some $140 million because of, to quote Mr. Griffith, chairman of Stelco, the unfavourable tax climate and other things. It seems to me very strange that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has embarked on a program of pouring millions of dollars into various industries, some of which in my opinion are so harebrained that they do not have a chance in the world of succeeding.
The government has put up 20 per cent or 30 per cent of the capital cost of some of these ventures in the hope they will provide jobs at a cost of $1,000, $2,000, $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 each. On the other hand, we have a situation like Wabush Mines where the company has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the operation and is now contemplating a big expansion but cannot go ahead with it because of the general tax climate. When this postponement became public knowledge the Minister of Finance very glibly said the company had not come to him for assistance. He said if they did so, he would be glad to talk to them but they had not made representations so we would have to wait.
I do not think that is good enough. The Iron Ore Company of Canada is operating largely with United States capital, and a good deal of the capital of Wabush Mines is U.S., but I cannot go along with this attitude of the government. I cannot go along with the idea that we can afford the luxury of telling the United States, Germany, France or other countries that we are masters of our own destiny and do not want their money. I feel so strongly about it that I would call this attitude irresponsible. Every time I hear this suggestion it reminds me of the story about the flea crawling up the elephant's back, intent on rape.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You mean the mouse.

Perhaps it was a mouse, but with a flea it would be more dramatic and even more difficult. Seriously, I cannot go along with that suggestion because I have seen the conditions which exist in certain parts of the country. While Ontario may have reached its apex, along
November 23, 1971

with parts of the west, in Newfoundland we have not reached the luxurious position of being able to turn down capital or take it only on our own terms. I think it was the president of Industrial Acceptance who said some months ago that a dollar knows no nationality or, if you want, a buck is a buck. I find it hard to sit quietly and listen to these suggestions of irresponsible people who think we can control our own destiny.
I wonder how much foreign investment these people have already discouraged as a result of such irresponsible remarks. How many firms, groups and consortiums have wanted to invest in Canada but because of this kind of talk and fears as to the crazy laws this crazy government might pass have not taken a chance? This can be compared to the situation which still exists in Quebec because of the threat of separation. This threat has discouraged all kinds of investment in that province; no one there will deny that. Such idle, irresponsible talk has created this problem in Quebec.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion has had to use funds designed for less affluent areas of the country to entice back to Quebec some of the industries the province has lost. They have used these funds throughout the province, but also in the city of Montreal. This is a very serious situation. I cannot buy the suggestion that this country of 20 million people does not want U.S. or other foreign investment.
At this point I am speaking specifically about the area of Labrador, in the province of Newfoundland, and my riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. Here we have an area of some 110,000 square miles. Common sense tells us that Labrador City, Wabush and other areas were developed because of United States investment in projects such as the air force base which we are thankful is in our province.
Then there is a swing of people along the coast of Labrador who live in semi-primitive conditions. When I go into this area I see the difference between the conditions on the coast of Labrador and those in the ultra-modern towns of Wabush and Labrador City, where they have every amenity apart from a road to get out. They have a good airline, golf courses, curling rinks and decent, well heated homes.
And good bars.

And good bars, if you like. I do not care where the investment comes from. People in Ontario, part of the west and parts of Quebec may say they do not want any foreign investment, but I can say from experience that we want this investment and we do not give a damn where it comes from. A buck is a buck. We have a huge territory in Labrador. As I have said, I cannot go into the specifics of this bill because I would not know what I was talking about. However, with this huge territory and its riches in ores, common sense indicates that this government owes it to the people of Canada and to people of our province to provide every possible incentive to see that the territory is developed and not discouraged.
As I mentioned earlier, there is the example of Wabush Mines which abandoned its development plans involving
Income Tax Act
some $140 million, which would have meant so much to the area. They were hung up on the government's indecision and on the threat of this terrible white paper. The parliamentary secretary is yawning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Believe me, it is cumulative.

I can appreciate that. The problem as I and the majority of people of Canada see it is that this has been a government of confrontation. It seems the government has wanted to confront everybody with a white paper which staggers them so that they do not know whether they are coming or going. There would seem to be an attitude of hit the Catholics, hit the Protestants, hit the French, hit the English and everybody with the threat of the white paper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member care to clarify his "hit the Catholics, hit the Protestants" statement?

I do not think the parliamentary secretary should be so sensitive. It is a figure of speech. I could have said hit the Russians and every other organized group with a white paper that would stun them. I say this is a cowardly way to govern, and the parliamentary secretary knows this. A government that is elected by the people should have the intestinal fortitude to govern without trying to cover every track they make politically. The government should be prepared to introduce tax changes which would encourage investment. It should do this on its own initiative and not after meetings with labour and businessmen of the country, and other types of cowardly actions.
Cowardice is what this is, and the signs are that the Canadian people are catching on to this. I think the parliamentary secretary knows this, despite my belief that he is doing a good job of bearing up under the pressure of this debate, although I doubt whether he knows very much more about the tax bill than I do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I concur with the last remarks of my hon. friend. Never did one poor, lone parliamentary secretary do such a reasonable job with so little to work on. I think he should be congratulated for that, especially when he has to push back-benchers to one side as they raise unruly heads of revolt against this bill. I think the parliamentary secretary is not doing a bad job under the circumstances.
I have a particular interest in this issue. I agree with what has been said on this side of the House, with a sharp distinction between my colleagues and any hon. friends to the left, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North when he spoke about poverty on one hand and wealth and industry on the other. Of course, that is the result of a mixed economy. We have a mixed economy, part of which is represented by individual incentive. Obviously, the part which is poverty stricken is that which is represented by the socialist aspect of the economy.
This is borne out by the fact that when we were dealing in this House a number of years ago with the question of developing the mining areas of the north and were seeking a policy, members of the government party-who were then members of the Official Opposition-strengthened by members of the New Democratic Party struggled

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
desperately against the attempt by the government to successfully develop these mining areas. When we attempted to bring wealth into the north it was the Liberal Party, aided by their kissing cousins, the New Democratic Party, which did all it could to stop the construction of the Pine Point railway which led not only to the development of the mining area but to incidental progress.
This is the point I want to make. I went into the north country well over 42 years ago. After seeing what the government is doing here, I sometimes think I should have stayed there. In any event, we knew there were resources. We talk about gas and oil. In 1920, 1921 and 1922 an attempt was made, using the tax laws as they then were, to develop the oil and gas resources which were within 40 or 50 miles of the town of Peace River. A few years before I arrived there a program had been launched by Imperial Oil and other local companies. There was no interest and no possibility of securing from eastern Canada the kind of capital that was required at that time. There was some local capital and know-how but it was completely inadequate because the people who had the capital in the central part of Canada said they would have nothing to do with the program. This stands as mute testimony of the abortive attempt to develop 50 years ago the gas and oil resources of that area-wells which had been capped and wells which had been running in tar for some time.
Going up and down the river, as I did for many years, travelling 300 or 400 miles into the north, I saw evidence that there must be an attractive policy with regard to our tax laws in order to maintain the steady flow of capital required to promote these resources. If we had waited for the Liberal government and the money which they were able to mobilize, nothing would have happened in the development of the mineral, gas and oil resources of northern Canada.
Not only what happens there, but the incidental effects are important. I spoke about the Pine Point mine which was opened up under a very acceptable agreement reached between the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the mining companies, the railroads and other people who were interested in developing the north and seeking out resources. People were prepared, when they saw evidence that a suitable climate was to be provided by the government under the tax laws and the agreements which were entered into-transportation agreements and those involving the construction of the railroad-to undertake this development.
This brings me to what the hon. member for Duvernay said, namely, let us cut out all expenditures for the development of our natural resources and concentrate on manufacturing and on what he calls the labour-intensive industries. I do not dismiss this, but I say to members of the committee that we no longer have the labour-intensive industries which we had some years ago. If this country is to remain competitive with regard to its manufacturing and industrial resources, it must do so on the basis of automation, economy through scientific improvement and the means we use to develop our manufacturing industries.
One need only examine the statistics of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to note the millions of dollars which have been spent. I will not go into the question of where they were spent-I would not be allowed to do so even if I wanted to-but it obviously takes a tremendous amount of money today compared with 20 or 30 years ago to develop jobs in the manufacturing industry, which apparently the hon. member for Duvernay is contemplating. That situation no longer applies. When you develop a natural resource such as gas, oil or minerals, there are incidental and ancillary effects which have a great impact upon our economy.
There is a farm just across the river from the town of Peace River. There is a hill there. When I first went to that country over 40 years ago I could stand on top of this hill, and look down and see no development. Just a few years before I arrived there, people were crossing the river by ferry. There was no highway to Edmonton. There was a railroad but only one train a week. There was no means of transportation to go north except boat to Hudson Bay. There were boats which went north during the brief navigation period in the summer. But after the benevolent policies of the Conservative government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-with the tax benefits which were available and the first-class agreements which were entered into-the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was then minister of northern affairs and did a great deal of work in this connection-immediately we saw not only the development of the mine at Pine Point but other incidental growth. Logging camps were established, mills developed, highways were built, bridges were built. Today I can go to the same hill, look down, and six miles away I see a modern airport at which jets can land. Because of the development of the gas and oil industry in the north, more planes are landing and taking off than at any other comparable place on the North American continent.
I see bridges built and highways going north. I see highways travelling into the north, and I see a railroad. From this hill I see where the railroad branches off and trains go into the Northwest Territories. These are things which lead to growth and to the employment of people as well as to the development of the great northern parts of our country.
I can hear the parliamentary secretary sighing. He may have heard all this before but it is about time someone on that side of the House listened and believed, because are the things which lead to the development and growth of the north, which is required-not the stultifying, limited sort of development-arising from the tax proposals which this bill envisages with relation to the gas and oil industry; not the kind of policies which this government envisages with regard to the development and flow of capital into this country.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to members of the committee that there is no one simple, magic formula which effectively deals with this problem. It needs a continuing influx of capital under conditions which must be acceptable to the people of Canada. It needs tax laws and a tax climate which will persuade people to invest in development. Too often in our tax laws we punish the

November 23, 1971

worthy, those whose efforts lead to growth, and we reward unduly the unworthy. These are matters which we must consider if we are to have tax laws and a tax climate which will lead to the development of the country, in particular that part of the country which I know well.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speechtext: Shall section 21 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I think I should put on record that the proposals affecting resource industries as they appear in Bill C-259 are substantially similar to those outlined in the white paper and as modified by the letter sent by the Minister of Finance on August 26, 1970, to the provincial ministers of finance.
The bill does go somewhat further in that it provides for the deduction of foreign exploration and development expenditures on a limited basis, an expanded qualification of mining assets eligible for a tax write-off and an extension of the 25 per cent depreciation allowance until 1976. Although these modifications of the white paper proposals may not appear to be very significant, they should be considered in light of the over-all fundamental changes proposed for the treatment of corporations and shareholders generally. As in the case of international taxation, the bill relies heavily on regulations which cannot be issued formally until the bill is enacted.
One of the great criticisms with respect to the resource industry is that most of the tax law governing it is imposed by regulation. In Parliament we have enacted statutes with provisions for the establishment of regulations. Parliament gives a wide ranging stamp of approval to certain principles and then cabinet writes the regulations. Therefore, so far as this debate is concerned it is difficult to determine what the law will be affecting resource industries because most of it is unwritten law and unwritten law is the most dangerous because such law can be changed at any time without Parliament's approval or knowledge.
Having said that I would like to point out that resource industries mean a lot to western Canada. The expansion of those industries, whether they be petroleum, coal or other mines, depends on the system of taxation governing them. By way of introduction, it is rather interesting to look at some of the history of the philosophy that prevails in western Canada. The Calgary Herald is the main newspaper in Calgary. It has the biggest circulation, along with the The Albertan.
It is the organ of truth.

That may well be so. It had this to say in 1867, and it is as true today as it was then:
The fisheries are a valuable property.
Income Tax Act
Then it went on to deal with trade with the United States, as follows:
Anything consistent with reason we are willing to grant to our neighbours; but it is rather hard to threaten to cut us off from the American continent simply because we are not prepared to yield them equal rights in a source of wealth which, on their own admission, belongs exclusively to us.
That may be too narrow a regional position, but it seems to me as I listen to debates in this House that we in Parliament are divided not so much by parties as by regions. I think that is quite true. If you listen to somebody from western Canada, they speak as a westerner and about the resources they have. The following appears at page 98:
In 1896 the Calgary Herald noted with approval that a candidate had said "let a man be either a Liberal or a Conservative, he must be a northwest man first"-
They use the term "northwest" when they mean a westerner.
-"and for party afterwards." . .. "Country before party."
This country is still divided basically by regions rather than political parties. We must have an amalgamation of interests across the board and such union creates political parties. Those interests, representing various regions, form the national purpose which makes this Parliament function.
As I said earlier, the health and growth of the economy of western Canada depends on the tax picture. The first anomaly that I notice in all the rules and regulations that have been and will be laid down is that some people think we can cut off foreign investment, that we can have a screening system. I have here a copy of the Herbert Gray report, whether legitimate or illegitimate-though nobody denied it during the question period.
It is a bastard.

The selective approach of this screening process determines how control of investment will be exercised-where it is going, to whom it is going, how it is going and when it is going to be made. A screening method, of course, is totally inadequate and irresponsible as far as western Canada is concerned.
The decision made a few days ago by the National Energy Board of Canada with reference to the export of natural gas to the United States has to be mentioned in this debate. It is rather interesting to read what the president of an oil company had to say on this matter. I know some who look with scepticism at presidents of oil companies-
Right.

You say "Right", but I do not want to get into an argument with you. I do not look with scepticism at any organization, whether union or corporate. As I have said before, corporations are healthy, and when they operate in a tax climate that gives them help we can have some degree of full development and full employment. That should be the aim. The president of Imperial Oil Limited, Mr. J. A. Armstrong, is quoted in an article in
November 23, 1971

Income Tax Act
the Winnipeg Free Press of Tuesday, November 23, 1971, as follows:
-warned Monday of serious political and economic effects if Canadians submit to the "myth" that Canada's oil and natural gas should not be exported to the United States, but preserved for domestic use.
J. A. Armstrong called the revenue effects of a decision not to export "disastrous". He plegged the immediate revenue loss at over $11 billion a year and said it would hit both the Canadian petroleum industry and the governments which are the royalty owners.
Naturally, in the west we are interested in royalties. When Mr. Douglas, the former leader of the NDP, was Premier of Saskatchewan he realized then, as Premier Schreyer realizes now, that foreign capital is needed for the development of resources and for full employment. Mr. Douglas said that, and Mr. Schreyer made it very clear on television the other night. But I do not want to digress, Mr. Chairman. The article continues:
The political effects would arise from a reminder that the United States supplied Canada with petroleum until the mid-fifties and on an emergency basis after the closure of the Suez Canal.
The worst consequence of a decision not to export Canadian resources would be the effect on investment spending. Mr. Armstrong said. "The investment spending by private industry would dry up completely and there is no conceivable set of conditions or incentives that government could provide that would prevent this from happening."
Mr. Armstrong said that Canada has two options-to develop or to stagnate its petroleum industry. He called a decision to sit back and refuse to export resources and concentrate on production for the domestic market a vote for stagnation.
"With the world's largest growing market for petroleum energy at our doorstep and with the great potential for crude and natural gas development in the frontiers, it would be a catastrophe if Canada does not capitalize on this unique opportunity not only to strengthen its economy but to assure itself of a plentiful and secure supply of oil and gas in a very uncertain world," he said.
The National Energy Board Friday turned down applications to export some 2.66 trillion cubic feet of natural gas to the United States.
I pause there, Mr. Chairman. Prior to these applications coming before the National Energy Board they were examined by the Alberta Conservation Board. The decision of the National Energy Board questions whether we have enough natural gas to meet Canada's domestic and industrial needs forseeable for the future. In the Borden report our proven reserves were estimated at 23 trillion cubic feet. According to the National Energy Board we do not have that kind of reserve, and if this is so then the way to get the reserve is through development. The way to encourage development is by an attractive tax climate. The reserves are there in the ground.
That leads me to a few more quotations from the remarks of the president of Imperial Oil. Commenting on the board's decision, Mr. Armstrong said:
-there is a difference of opinion in Canada as to the surplus of natural gas in the immediate future.
I agree with the Prime Minister on a point of law. If the National Energy Board makes an affirmative decision, the cabinet can approve or negate it. That is sound law, and in that regard the Prime Minister stands on all fours with the National Energy Board Act. However, if the decision is negative, the cabinet may not be able to change it. The only recourse is appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada under section 18 of the National Energy Board

Act on a question of law or a question of jurisdiction, which does not help us in this field.
At the moment we are debating the tax bill, whether we are going to get development and what kind of tax climate we will have in light of the fact that the National Energy Board turned down applications to export natural gas worth $11 billion each year. That is half a billion dollars more than the new budget for the whole of Canada.
Having, in my opinion, quoted the law correctly the Prime Minister should now take two decisions. First, the government should ask the National Energy Board to review its decision. In the event that the board maintains its decision, the government should review the tax climate of this nation, because it is stagnating development in our country and that is why we have unemployment to the degree that now exists. I want to be very positive and that is why I make these suggestions.
Second, since the act does not permit the cabinet to review decisions which negative or turn down applications, I hope the government will bring the members of that board before the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources so that parliamentarians may examine them. Their decision came as a shock to western Canada and should be shocking to all Canadians. We want to determine on what basis they estimated reserves and if they think that, given the tax climate which is being discussed in this debate, reserves will increase.
I hope the members of the board will be called before the committee. I should like the privilege of cross-examining the chairman of the board and its members. If anyone says that would be an unusual procedure, I say hogwash. On previous occasions when the standing committee has asked for it, those gentlemen have appeared before the committee. I have often recommended in committee and to the government that the staff of the board be increased to a level that is commensurate with the board's responsibilities under the National Energy Board Act.
In light of the tax climate being created today and the resulting uncertainty, I recommend, first, that the government ask the National Energy Board to review its decision. It should bear in mind the revenue that can be generated in Canada as a result of developments within the industry. I am speaking of benefits which will come from tertiary industries and from exports.
I recommend, second, that the gentlemen of the board be called before the standing committee so the committee may examine them and find out exactly why they decided to veto the decision of the Conservation Board of Alberta. When we have heard the evidence we can say whether that decision should stand or fall. To me, coming from western Canada, the board's decision is shocking. The royalties from this industry which flow to provincial governments of western Canada, and the revenues that indirectly flow into the coffers of the federal government, are substantial. Therefore, when legislating new tax laws we must be very careful.
I now continue quoting what Mr. Armstrong is reported to have said, according to the Winnipeg Free Press:
"The United States only takes our reserves for security because we're close. One or two more tankers from the Persian Gulf to the U.S. market and we're out," he answered.
November 23, 1971

By 1980, he estimated that Canada would be supplying about 4 to 5 per cent of U.S. demand for oil and gas.
We went to bed, so to speak with one-eighth of the world's supply of coal in Alberta. All the arguments that my friends to the left raised in this debate were raised years ago. They sound wonderful on the hustings, but they are no good for employment. They are beautiful for winning votes, but no good for the economy of the country or the economic well-being of the average man. We went to bed in the twenties and the thirties with our coal; and who in Alberta or anywhere else in Canada now wants to go to bed with our natural gas? I continue quoting:
Mr. Armstrong estimated capital requirements of the developing Canadian petroleum resources in the next decade at $25 to $30 billion.
The article refers to $25 to $30 billion. That sounds like a lot of money. A capital gains tax is to be introduced through this bill and, while it sounds good on paper, it will rob the average Canadian of any incentive to invest in resources. That is the anomaly of it. It may be funny; my expression of going to bed with our gas. I think it is funny and I said some time ago that it was funny. One sometimes has to show how funny a thing is in order to demonstrate how tragic it is.
Having said in my opening remarks that the regulations I am talking about are similar in nature to those contemplated in the white paper, let me show what the great experts said in committee. I am about to read excerpts taken from official report No. 33 of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. These proceedings took place on April 16, 1970, at 3.40 in the afternoon. I should like to put some questions and answers on the record because my hon. friend opposite from Calgary felt that the answers were not as suggested in another debate. Actually, we were debating another section of the bill. I directed my first question to Mr. Bryce, the economic adviser to the Prime Minister. I asked, "Did you assist in the drafting of the proposals." Mr. Bryce answered: Normally the government does not reveal who did what within it, but it is well known that Mr. Brown and I did assist in drafting these proposals.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee agree unanimously to the hon. member continuing?
Agreed.

I appreciate the committee's courtesy, Mr. Chairman. I will not be unduly lengthy. I can speak again after an interval. My party has asked me to place on record a few facts which are important to western Canada and to Canada as a whole. My next question was: Does the white paper proposal on taxation abolish the distinction between capital gains and income, and treat capital gains as ordinary taxable income?
Let me digress for a moment. The United States and Great Britain have capital gains taxes. Farmers I was talking to the other night in Manitoba were shocked to hear that any capital gains they made would be added to their income and that half those gains would be taxed at
Income Tax Act
ordinary income tax rates. Yet here we are dealing with the resource industry. Surely we want to encourage economic development. How will that development come about if you say to investors in resource industries, "We will take the cream off the top of the milk in the can and all you will have left "is skim milk". And then you are asked to make butter. Out of what?
That is how ridiculous this law is and that is what it will do to our resource industries. I know that my friends to the left say that the white paper did not go far enough. They found out exactly how far the white paper went only when its proposals affected the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. They did not think they would lose any rural seats in Saskatchewan.
But we have just won a seat.

Sometimes it takes a little time for the correct facts to be known. The rest of my question was as follows:
For example; if a person has a taxable income of earned $10,000 from wages, and earns $10,000 on the stock market, what is the rate of tax on $10,000 capital gains?
Mr. Brown answered:
Half of it will bear the progressive rate as if that gain was a taxable income today.
In other words, one half of the capital gain will be taxed at progressive income tax rates. The provisions of the white paper basically have been incorporated in Bill C-259, so that when you talk about the white paper you are talking about Bill C-259. I then asked whether the capital gain would not be added to taxable income in that year. Mr. Brown answered, "Yes, sir." Actually, I asked the following:
An ordinary landholder who bought some land, then sold it and in that taxable year, whatever year it might be, he made $10,000.1 am asking you, under the ordinary rules, would not that capital gain be added to his taxable income in that one year?
Mr. Brown answered, "Yes, sir." I then asked:
Yes, so basically, although you have mentioned some exceptions and I am prepared to determine those in a few moments, what the chartered accountant of one of the national firms said is true, that the distinction between capital gains and income will be virtually abolished because in many cases-I have given you two or three illustrations, but I am sure you could give me more than I have given you because you are far more knowledgeable in this field-it will merely be added to the taxable income and become taxable in that year. Is that correct?
Mr. Brown answered, "Yes, it is." Mr. Chairman, I want to drive this point home because it is important to farmers and to those investing in the resource industries. Half of any capital gain is to be included in income and will be taxed at progressive income tax rates. What are those progressive rates? They are not 25 per cent or less, as in the United States or Great Britain. They run as high as 61 per cent in Canada, a new country. And then some Members of Parliament say we do not need foreign investment! That is the anomaly I see under this tax bill.
How can hon. members, no matter on which side of the House they sit, believe that we do not need foreign investment? We are going to ask Canadians to invest in their industry and at the same time tax them on capital gains at

I would like to ask a question related to investment and unemployment. The hon. member said that one of the reasons we have such a high level of unemployment is that we are not encouraging investment. My recollection is that in 1960, 1961 and 1962, when the

hon. member's party had some responsibility for governing this country, we had a rate of unemployment of something over 10 per cent. At that time we had far greater incentives to investment in Canada: we had a dollar that was rising rapidly. How does the hon. member relate that to unemployment?

We took office in 1956. I do not want to get into a side issue. I am not here to defend, but I shall answer. I am not here to defend what happened to Mackenzie King, Bennett, Diefenbaker, or anybody else. I am debating a tax bill and what in my opinion is sound economics. But I can answer the question. The hon. member knows as well as I do that when we took office in 1956 there was unemployment.

Yes, 1957. But 1956 was the beginning. There was unemployment in the United States as well as in Canada. Mr. Sharp and Mr. Winters both admitted on the election platform that unemployment had dropped to lower than 6 per cent by 1962 because of the programs put into effect by the Diefenbaker government.
Hear, hear!

I am not going to get into side issues. That is when the boom started. If the hon. member for Waterloo wants to go back 20 or 30 years I would ask him, why did Clarence Fines, the CCF provincial treasurer, leave Saskatchewan with approximately $3 million? I do not know. Answer that one. Why did some become very rich? They were socialists and were preaching that religion across the land. I could ask other questions but nobody has a monopoly on political morality in this House. I again quote:
Mr. Bryce, thinking of the questions that I have put and the answers Mr. Brown had made to those questions, it is possible under the white paper that for a period Canadians could pay as high as 80 per cent capital gains tax under certain circumstances. I will give you an example, if there is any question about that.
I gave him an example. Mr. Bryce replied:
Oh, on certain transactions, in the first year of the new system as proposed, yes.
For two years we debated the white paper. For two years investment and business in this country were threatened. They were threatened until this bill was introduced. Now the rate is up to 61 per cent. We were threatened with a tax on capital gains, on investment of possibly 80 per cent. In light of the atmosphere since this government took office, scaring away development, investment and exploration, how can our economy not be stagnated at this time?
If the National Energy Board says we do not have enough resources, I do not agree with them. But they have the jurisdiction. As a parliamentarian, I have only the right to criticize. I want them to appear before the committee so I can hear their evidence. If there are not the reserves, the answer is to put capital and men to work. You cannot have prosperity and economic development when you are stagnating industry by taking away Canadian capital. The government says it can do things better. It says it will handle the money. That is the record of what took place in committee.

Under our tax law, much of the tax treatment of the oil industry is contained in regulations. It appears that this concept is carried forward in Bill C-259. The concept that I have read from the white paper has been carried into the resource industry, although the government has seen fit to issue a series of vague proposed regulations since the white paper of November 7, 1969. Most of the regulations proposed by the oil industry were included in a news release by the Department of Finance on July 6 of this year. These regulations are permissible-this is referred to in sections 65 and 66 of Bill C-259-but they are not included in the bill. It is the intention to evaluate these proposed regulations with full understanding; however, they are likely to be changed. Obviously, anticipation of such changing regulations has contributed in some measure to the present instability in our business community.
Before making an assessment of the proposed tax regulations, it may be appropriate at this point to discuss some aspects of Canada's present energy position-I have already discussed certain of these aspects-and consider the manner in which a restrictive tax treatment can greatly influence Canada's future position. At a time when more and more Canadians are concerned with the future of Canadian independence, little is being done by the government to encourage the investment of private risk capital to develop our resource frontiers. That, basically, is the weakness of the tax policy presented to us. Particular reference is made to the existence of drilling funds which under United States tax laws favour the use of essentially private capital in a risk-taking venture, such as oil or gas explorations, by granting certain incentives to individuals willing to take such risks.
My next recommendation is this: Our tax laws in relation to the resource industries should offer far more incentives that the United States system because we are competing against the United States capital. If we can create a better atmosphere we could hope to attract Canadian investment in Canadian industry on a larger scale. The end would be achieved not by regulation but by the individual initiative. This is one of the factors which should have been considered when this bill was in preparation, particularly with regard to competition in the resource industry. Remember, when we are dealing with a resource industry we are dealing with an international industry. I have heard people say it is a terrible thing that it should be international. But of course it is international. It is international because oil, natural gas and minerals are found almost everywhere in the world. The companies concerned must operate in various countries in order to remain in a competitive position and be able to pay a fair wage to their employees and provide a fair standard of working conditions.
Through a fair system of tax write-offs and depletion allowances, United States tax laws have created a means by which individual Americans can participate not only in the development of domestic resource frontiers but also in the development of Canadian resources. If Canadians are concerned about the influence of foreign control over some of our industries, then establishment of Canadian tax laws providing parity incentives for private risk capi-
Income Tax Act
tal is a necessary prerequisite to give Canadians the opportunity to invest in their own resources.
We should make Canadian industry fully competitive. We talk about foreign investment but we refuse to give the same competitive shake to Canadians. What kind of law is this? What kind of economic system is that? When you read just one side of the story it sounds good. Thank goodness that in justice, whether it is economic or judicial justice, there are two sides to every story. Quite obviously, a fair competitive basis with comparable tax incentives for Canadians is a much better means of giving Canadians the opportunity to gain or preserve control of their resource industries than the presently proposed screening mechanism of the government.
Let us look at this proposed screening mechanism, a description of which is to be found at page 21 of "The Canadian Forum"-the leak! This is a government of many leaks. In my submission it is one big leak after another. The Secretary of State for External Affairs should be called the chief of many leaks. The following is what it said about the screening process:
A screening process could be the least protectionist and hence the least costly of the possible policy alternatives because of its flexibility. It could, in fact, contribute to the efficiency of the Canadian economy. It could seek to reverse procurement decisions which were based on arbitrary and non-economic factors which contribute neither to the welfare of the particular Canadian firm nor to the country as a whole.
I pause here. Would any provincial or federal government in existence in the forties, before Leduc No. 1 was brought in by Imperial Oil to give us the first major oilfield in Alberta, have agreed to put money into that project? Here I agree with the Prime Minister. I have already quoted the Prime Minister twice tonight with approval, something which is rare for me. The right hon. gentleman said this country was run by a group of experts and not by parliamentarians elected by the Canadian people. Well, I do not want a bunch of bureaucrats determining whether a well should be drilled for natural gas or petroleum, because I do not trust their judgment. In the field of incentive, people take risks, sink mines, drill shafts and create economic growth which brings jobs for men and women. That is what incentive is about.
Hear, hear!

At a time when we are talking about unemployment every day, the government is considering setting up a system of selection to determine through a government agency or somebody in the public service where, when and in what manner funds should be invested. I think the history of western Canada might have shown very little development if policies of this kind had been decided in some office in an ivory tower. I think the parliamentary secretary would agree with me, because I read some remarks he made recently relative to the export of gas. This is why I say we are divided in this House by regions, on occasion, rather than by narrow, party politics. I read further:
In those cases where procurement from the parent is in the best interests of the firm but not necessarily in the best interests of the long-term economic development of Canada, a screening process could bargain for the location of the next expansion in Canada in cases where this is economic.

Does any hon. member believe for one moment that the Sudbury mines would have been found by bureaucrats sitting in an ivory tower? Do they really believe there would today be an oil and gas industry in Alberta if decisions had been left to some bureaucrat? I do not believe so. It was only in the field of competition, through the interplay of action, knowledge and investment that the growth of this country took place right from the Mari-times to Victoria. Development has gone on in this country on such a scale in the last hundred years as to be unrivalled anywhere except perhaps in the United States.
And where did it get us?
I don't know where it got you. But I do not want to get off target. I shall not listen to a lot of nonsense.
We are having to.

Everybody has a right to take part in this debate. I have only spoken once, and I felt I should enter into the discussion at this point. If hon. members disagree with me, I shall be happy to listen to them carefully.

The new production facilities in Canada could serve, for example, the Canadian and European markets with the MNE acting as a channel for Canadian exports to European subsidiaries. The extent to which the screening process can secure this type of investment for Canada will depend upon many factors including the costs of production, access to foreign markets, transportation costs, etc.
All the factors will be put through a computer. But the information fed into a computer is only as good as the knowledge that goes with it. Does anyone imagine we could have achieved our present economic growth had the suggested screening method been in operation? I recall the days when Mr. Pearson criticized my right hon. friend from Prince Albert during the years he was Prime Minister for taking initiative in the development of the north. Let us suppose Mr. Pearson had still been in the public service and had been given the job of deciding whether or not any development in the north should take place. All we would ever have up there would be igloos. And if we had taken that kind of advice, the CPR would never have been built. The Grits said it would never pay for the cost of the axle grease.
Whenever we get rules and regulations and people interpreting them, we should look out because expansion is likely to be nil. That is what is wrong with this tax bill. That is why I refer to the tax bill and its link with screening and regulation. We have reached a point in this country where we have an NDP government, because the Prime Minister and two of his henchmen sitting over there walked out of that party because of a deal, went over to the government party and took office as NDP members under the name of Liberals. That is what we have.
Hear, hear!

It does not make any economic sense to have this screening process that apparently seeks to ensure, for the Canadian supplier, an opportunity to compete for supply contracts. But that is what we are linked with in the tax bill. This bill is an unwritten book of regulations. When the regulations are written, unless they are leaked to us they are hidden laws. That is the only way we find out about them, because we cannot pry answers from the government.
A glance at the proposed tax amendments and regulations of Bill C-259 immediately raises the question, what are these measures intended to achieve in the energy sector of our economy? Let me deal with Canadian energy policy as it fits into taxation. Predictions for the remainder of this decade are that the demand for minerals and energy resources will accelerate at an unprecedented rate. By 1980 the United States will consume over 80 per cent of the world's mineral and energy resources. That figure is based on what an economist says. Canada, through its proximity and close affiliation to United States markets, must formulate a Canadian resource policy. Perhaps it is time we had a national resource policy, but such policy must attract Canadian companies to develop our own resources for Canadians.
I do not know what is meant by a continental energy policy but I have always maintained that this was dangerous. Deals have been worked out, like the national oil policy, whereby we permit the eastern market, divided by the Ottawa Valley, to obtain crude oil from other countries provided we can serve the northwestern United States market. We started off by supplying that market with 250,000 barrels of crude per day, with a target of 800,000 barrels per day. We managed to achieve the goal of 800,000 barrels per day, and even the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources admits that. If a decision arrived at is such that in the near future central Canada needs more natural gas and energy than was estimated, then let us get on the job and build pipelines to bring it here. Let us survey central Canada to find out whether more energy is needed. If more energy is needed, .let us obtain signed purchase contracts so that western Canada can then properly assess the need. The need could properly be assessed by the National Energy Board and the Alberta Conservation Board. In any event, let us make an assessment now of our energy requirements.
You can take gas to the Maritimes.

Yes, we could take gas to the Maritimes. In order to have the kind of vitality we need in the industry, we must have a tax atmosphere which encourages investment, and we must have markets. I say, let us build the pipelines to the eastern market. If we are to be nationalists in respect of one area, we must be nationalists across the board. We have pools of natural gas and petroleum in Alberta and it may be that policies can be worked out to supply eastern markets. This is a field for the experts, not for parliamentarians. But if we are to have a national policy we must work out some deals. If we are to keep our gas in the ground waiting for something to happen somewhere else, then surely we have a right to build a pipeline and market crude petroleum and crude natural gas in the Montreal area. In this way we could keep the western economy healthy.
