I have made several recommendations not only in respect of taxation but in respect of markets. In relation to this question it is interesting to read what was written recently in a Winnipeg paper:
Government economists as soothsayers have a very mixed reputation. We have been, throughout our history, a capital-short nation. It was rather generally assumed, until recently, that for purposes of development-which is very important to national unity-we needed all the savings we could get, both domestic and foreign. The revised view evidently is that, in the domestic sense, we are much stronger than we assumed and that foreign capital, although it should not necessarily be excluded, is something to be feared and screened and regulated. It is at Canada's door pressing to get in and the role of a protective government must be to admit it only on prescribed conditions. In similar fashion, we screen immigrants lest subversives or insufficiently close relatives gain access to the country.
But the the economists may be at fault in their readings of the signs and portents. In a brief submitted last week to the Ontario securities commission, two brokerage firms made two points rather forcefully. The first was that Canadian demand for both debt and equity capital will increase significantly in the next decade. The second was that the United States, far from attempting to force investment upon us, may be more disposed to end the privileged exemption from the interest equalization tax which Canadian issues have enjoyed since 1963 and from other restrictions on direct foreign investment imposed in 1968 on U.S. firms. If these propositions are sound, the government has brought itself to the present somewhat embarrassing situation by tackling the wrong problem in the wrong way at the wrong time.
I will deal with another subject later, but those are my final words at this time. We are tackling the bill at the wrong time, and we are doing so at the expense of development, when we have high unemployment and a high cost of living. We have economic stagnation and a problem with the United States in respect of the surtax. We have a floating dollar which is just about at par with the U.S. dollar. We are putting our industry at a great disadvantage.
If we are to have full employment in this country we must have expansion. It does not take an economist to figure that out. To get expansion we must have investment in the resource industry. This industry needs large amounts of capital in order to find the resources and get them to the market. You can only obtain the capital with which to find the resources if you have a tax climate which encourages Canadians to invest in their own resources.
In addition, Canadians should have a better deal in the tax world than foreign investors in Canada. Under this bill they are put at a great disadvantage. This is shown by the questions and answers I read. This bill should go back to the drafting board. I have seen fights in caucus. I have never been in cabinet, but I assume the same fights go on there. This may be a fight between interests in one region and those in others, or interests in one group. But if we can succeed in what we must do we will attain expansion and full employment.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams), to the effect that Bill C-259 certainly does not promote individual initiative nor private enterprise. This
Income Tax Act
bill results naturally from the white paper tabled several months ago already and which did not seem to please the Canadian taxpayers as a whole. Whether the matter under consideration be section 21 or any other provision of this bill, we are faced with a tax reform which consists of taking away from those who have in order to try to give a little to those who have less. And by applying that policy, I suggest that we will surely come to a situation whereby more and more will have nothing and fewer and fewer will have something.
And if the government wonders why Canadians are hesitant to invest in new industries or in secondary industries, or to increase their production, it is simply because they are not interested in wasting their time for the pleasure of paying taxes.
We are complaining that, in the mining sector, for example, companies have to shut down because they are taxed too heavily. We have typical examples of this situation in northwestern Quebec. There are other examples in northeastern Ontario and in the Sudbury area.
Everywhere, in every area, people are disgusted, discouraged, and they cannot be blamed indeed.
We, of the Social Credit, have asked for many years that the income tax be reduced, and the ensuing decrease in income compensated by new credits created by the Bank of Canada. Of course, some find this amusing, and we keep on asking the Americans to come and invest here. We are surprised to see that they are increasingly embarrassed to invest in Canada because taxes are too high. In fact, some American companies now say they are willing to go back to the United States, and to sell from there their products to Canada, for it will cost them less to produce over there.
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe any of us can work miracles. One thing is sure, though: we hear more and more people say that we should take over the control of our national economy; more and more members of the NDP, of the Progressive Conservative party, and even of the Liberal party say: Let us take back the control of our economy. At the same time, the Prime Minister of Canada (M. Trudeau) says that 60 or 70 per cent of our economy is in the hands of Americans. Why? Because such a system was set up. The saints in Heaven or Brother Andre did not suggest that we ask the Americans for permission to develop our natural resources. And let us make no bones about it, because our Canadian companies, the Quebec, Ottawa or Manitoba governments go and beg in the United States for funds to develop hydro-electric projects. Manitoba and Quebec, for example, have borrowed $50 and $75 million respectively. The premiers of those two provinces do not come back from the United States with a bag full of American dollars. They come back with figures and promissory notes for the reimbursement to the United States of $75 million by Quebec and $50 million by Manitoba.
Mr. Chairman, the Americans do not base their $75 million on their wealth, but on the development of our resources. This is why, we say: Why are those figures written by Americans when they could have been written by the Bank of Canada? Those then would be figures that belonged to us and not to others, and that is the only way to regain control of our economy.

Income Tax Act
Yesterday, I heard the Quebec Premier, Mr. Bourassa, state that the James Bay development, which will cost $6 billion, will permit us to finally become masters of our economic destiny. Where shall we find those $6 billion? Mr. Bourassa gives the answer: In the United States. If the Americans finance the James Bay development, to whom will it belong? To us or to American financiers? We will still be in the same hole!
So, I ask those who have drafted Bill C-259: If the Americans can write those figures for the development of James Bay which belongs to us, why is Mr. Rasminsky not able to write some? Does he lack knowledge? Can he not add? Can he not state clearly that we can make the figures agree with the development of our natural resources? It is not a question of writing any figures, as the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) takes pleasure in repeating throughout the province of Quebec, but figures based on something real, that is the development of our natural resources.
Mr. Chairman, we have been discussing this famous tax bill for months. We consider it by groups of clauses, in order to take a little money from some to try and give it to others. About 80 per cent of everything that will be collected will be used to pay a larger bureaucracy, one that will keep us still more ignorant, and this, because we do not want to tackle the root of the problem. We stagnate, we procrastinate in the present system, and here in this House, members spend their time repeating speeches, quoting figures, when the legislation aims simply at confiscating private property and destroying personal initiative.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to personal income tax, the government said it could not afford to set the exemption at $5,000 for married people and at $3,000 for single persons.
Recently, the Senate Committee on Poverty published a report which may be related to Bill C-259, since its aim is to eradicate poverty in Canada and to provide a guaranteed annual income. For 35 years we have been calling this the vital minimum. Senator Croll just found out that we must come to that. The Prime Minister believes that a guaranteed annual income makes sense but that we cannot afford it. The hon. member for Papineau and the Minister of National Health and Welfare repeat the same thing: We cannot afford to do it, it would cost too much!
Mr. Chairman, should a war break out tomorrow, the question of millions or billions of dollars would be put aside. We would get into it to the limit of our physical capabilities. Financing would be available to the extent of our possibilities. We would not ask ourselves: Can we afford it? We would be told instead: This is an emergency!
Mr. Chairman, the present situation is one of emergency since terrorism is closing in and revolutionaries are disrupting the country. In fact, when we witness complete dissatisfaction at all levels of society, I say we are in a situation of national emergency.
We say that, in this country, everything that is physically feasible should be financially possible through the use of our financial institution par excellence, the Bank of Canada. That does not mean we should nationalize the

chartered banks. Not at all! Let them operate with private enterprise. But the government should take its responsibilities with regard to the public sector of our national economy.
What did the provinces, municipalities and school boards talk about when they met with the Prime Minister last week? What matters were discussed? Did they talk about the constitution? No! The Constitution is something like moving fine amendments, like talking literature to a poor chap who is dying of hunger! He does not listen too carefully, because he is not interested in literature or sweet nothings. When he is hungry, he wants to work and to earn a decent living.
What were the provinces talking about? Bill C-259. Even if they do not say it too often, all provinces face the same problem: lack of money. And the federal government shows up with a bill of some 725 pages to inform us that it has no more money than the provinces.
Thus, as the conference came to an end after three days, the representatives of the provinces went home, thinking: We had three days of discussions and we will meet again in three or six months. What for? In order to say: we still have no money. Let Ottawa give us some. Let them tax Canadians and give us what the money collected. All the provinces are asking for a better distribution of public funds in every field.
Mr. Chairman, we have have those federal-provincial conferences for ten or twelve years, but they did not solve anything because the federal government has the last word when it comes to credit and currency. The Constitution gives the federal government complete jurisdiction-through Parliament, of course-over matters of currency and credit, and this is why we say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), to the Prime Minister, to the government and to its members that the public sector of our economy-provinces, municipalities, school boards, and so on-should be financed through interest-free loans granted by the Bank of Canada. Provinces, municipalities and school boards would then have a chance to be more creative and to promote private enterprise and individual initiative.
I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that the bill will solve anything, even if it is carried unanimously. It does not contain any solution. We have to prevent this outdated system from exploiting us as it is doing at present.
A while ago, I mentioned a $75 million loan obtained by the Quebec government from the United States only a few weeks ago at the interest rate of 91 per cent over 25 years. Over 25 years, we shall have paid $225 million in interest only and still owe $75 million.
Now, on exactly the same day the Quebec government borrowed in the United States, Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, representing the federal government in the underdeveloped countries assistance program, was in India and granted that country a $40 million interest-free loan, refundable after 60 years. However, 60 years hence, the Prime Minister will be 113 years old, which means that he will no longer be here.
Mr. Chairman, again I am in favour of assistance to foreign countries, but if we are in a position to provide interest-free loans to India, why can we not also provide

interest-free loans to the city of Hull or to the provinces of Manitoba, Quebec and Saskatchewan?
More recently, we granted Yugoslavia a $140 million loan I believe, for a hydroelectric project or for setting up a TV broadcasting system. Apparently we can afford that. In fact, a foreign visitor to Canada never goes back home without a generous loan from the federal government.
As for the provinces, they have to go back empty-handed, not richer than they were before. And we call this a Canadian government for the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, I am not surprised to see the government's popularity going down in western Canada, where I was last week. I am not surprised to see the government loosing seats in by-elections as we have seen recently. I am not surprised either to find the people thoroughly disgusted, because there is nothing to offer except taxation bills to take away from those who have very little to give to those who have nothing.
Mr. Chairman, we will not go very far this way. I said earlier that we are in a national emergency situation and this is true. Nobody is happy. The students, the fathers and mothers, the handicapped, the pensioners, the senior citizens, the private businessmen are not happy. I am receiving many letters from business executives who complain that the government is eroding their profits and is compelling them to borrow money at exceedingly high interest rates to keep on operating. I said earlier that the province of Quebec is paying an interest rate of 9? per cent to the United States; the Bank of Canada has just cut its rate down to 41 per cent. I recently asked the Minister of Finance why the provinces should not be allowed to borrow from the Bank of Canada at 43 per cent instead of having to borrow from the United States at 91 per cent. The minister replied that such was the consensus. We must accept things as they are. Under the law the Bank of Canada has the right to make loans to the provinces, but only for a period not exceeding six months whereas New York financiers may make loans for 25, 40 or 50 years. All we would have to do would be to replace the words "six months" in the Bank of Canada Act by 25, 30, 35 or 40 years. That is the only thing to do. The Minister of Finance knows that but he has not got the courage to take his responsibilities, to so instruct the Bank of Canada. He knows the government has the power to instruct the Bank of Canada. Mr. Rasminsky also knows it quite well.
Mr. Chairman I am nearly through on the subject. Instead of introducing a bill of that nature and saying that we cannot afford to establish a social security system in Canada, let us try to see if Canada can produce enough to meet the needs of its population. This year the national output will total $90 billion and the national income will total $65 billion. How can we logically buy a production of $90 billion with an income of $65 billion? Ask the Minister of Finance or any economist in Canada. There is a difference of $25 billion between the production of Canada and its income when the stores, the factories and the warehouses are overflowing with all sorts of products. There is overproduction and we still hear people talking about increasing our production when we do not even have time to deal with the problem of distributing our wealth. The only way of achieving better distribution of our wealth in
Income Tax Act
Canada is to increase the purchasing power of the consumer by distributing a national dividend, as advocated by the Creditistes, and through a guaranteed minimum income, as was recently suggested by Senator Croll who only touched on the problem now facing Canada. When we are in a position to guarantee economic security, social security to the population as a whole then we will have fewer terrorists, revolutionaries, bomb blasts and disputes.
We have a solution, Mr. Chairman. In concluding my comments on Bill C-259,1 would state that even if we were to spend six months debating this legislation, it would not improve the economic situation of Canada nor would it generate a single new industry. On the contrary, existing industries are being driven out and prevented from expanding because people are being discouraged. And when someone is discouraged, nothing could entice him to take risks. It is precisely because nobody wants to take risks anymore that the government is taking away from us whatever we have. By avoiding risks, industries remain stagnant thus creating unemployment.
The unemployed are complaining. Even if new legislation provides increased unemployment benefits, the problem will not be solved. One or two years hence, we will still be facing the same situation because we will not have really come to grips with the problem.
The Creditistes have a suggestisn to offer. It matters very little whether the government considers it or not. One thing is certain which is that the Canadiin people are about to accept that solution to their greater advantage.

Mr. Chairman, I think members of this committee should be fully cognizant of the fact that when we are dealing with matters such as those presently before us we are dealing with national policy. We are determining what will happen to Canada and what kind of nation we will be in the future. Make no mistake about that, Mr. Chairman. I think no member of this House should be under any illusion in that respect. The policies we adopt as a result of this tax bill will influence the future of Canada. They will have a distinct effect upon what Canadians and other people do in Canada.
Earlier this evening the hon. member for Calgary North referred to action taken by governments in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, governments of the same political persuasion as my party. He pointed out that a former Premier of Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, had to take action to encourage oil development in that province. That is quite correct, Mr. Chairman. His government had to encourage oil development in Saskatchewan because of the framework within which national policies were operating. Under those national policies, agriculture-the basic industry of western Canada-was being ignored. Provincial services were being pinched and squeezed at every twist and turn. The cost of transportation in the west was constantly rising. All this was putting Saskatchewan and other prairie provinces in a real economic bind.
Under those national policies, secondary industry development was encouraged to remain away from western Canada. Those policies were structured in such a way that western Canada did not benefit from the development of

November 23, 1971
Income Tax Act
secondary industry. The government of Saskatchewan had to move to secure a piece of the action, to bring about the type of development that was so badly needed. I think it did a much better job than was being done at that time in other parts of Canada. It protected the people's interests. It devised new means of ensuring that the people of the province would get a fair return on their resources.
In particular the CCF government introduced the feature of the net royalty lease which resulted in oil companies large and small having an opportunity to get into the development picture. This also helped Canadian companies such as Co-op Refineries to take part in the oil game; and I may say that Canadian companies have not been able to play the same sort of role in other provinces. Here I refer to Alberta.
This is the type of policy we must follow in order to ensure that our people get a fair shake. But that policy was promptly cancelled by the Liberal government which took office in Saskatchewan in 1964. That government was more interested in getting a quick buck from the sale of leases or of particular parcels of land. Now I am happy to see that the new NDP government in the province of Saskatchewan is once again bringing into effect the net oil royalty lease program.
The hon. member for Calgary North also referred to statements made by the Premier of Manitoba. I listened to those statements when watching television. I point out that the Premier made it quite clear that if he had a choice between no development, between no investment and foreign investment, then in carrying out his responsibilities as Premier of the province he had no alternative but to ensure that there would be some degree of development by encouraging whatever foreign investment was necessary.
I think the hon. member for Calgary North and others who take a similar line of argument have missed the basic point-that responsibility rests here in Ottawa, in this Parliament, to ensure that there is an adequate national policy that will bring about the degree of development that we need and in a way that will work in the best interests of the Canadian people. We have a responsibility to ensure that that kind of development policy is carried out. We have never had an adequate development policy from either Liberal or Conservative governments.
When we look at the proposals placed before us in this bill concerning the basic resource industries of mining and petroleum, what do we find? We find special concessions. We find special deals that are available to no other sector of the Canadian economy. I ask the government, Mr. Chairman, to give me one example of how the proposals contained in this bill serve the principle of equity. Is there any degree of equity in the proposals concerning mining and petroleum? I suggest there is not. I predict that the Liberal government will rue the day they allow this bill to pass with the type of concessions contained in it. The people of Canada will realize what a sham this so-called tax reform legislation is.
Hear, hear!

The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that this bill is a gigantic giveaway, a sellout, handout of Canadian

resources and Canadian wealth. Let us compare what is being done for the giant oil companies and giant mining companies on the one hand, while on the other people interested in co-operatives and credit unions have to scramble in order to maintain any semblance of justice in their treatment under the proposed legislation. We debated this matter last week and I do not intend to go into it again now.
We have here a good example of the priorities of the Liberal government. They are prepared to give concessions and handouts to large corporations and cartels, but when it comes to an organization that is attempting to help people and where people are attempting to help themselves we find the government putting the squeeze on. What sort of justice is this? It will not produce the new, just society we heard so much about. Furthermore, when discussing the concessions contained in Bill C-259 as they affect basic resource industry, we must see how they influence economic development in Canada. I suggest they produce very serious and bad distortions of our economic development. I think we should keep this in mind.
In his remarks the hon. member for Calgary North said that if we ensure that there is good deal for the mining and petroleum companies, that will bring new jobs and new development and help to produce full employment. I believe I quote the sense of his statement correctly. But, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to the committee through you that more people in Canada are affected by the well-being and welfare of the co-operative and credit union movements in this country than are affected by the activities of the mining and petroleum industries.
Just where are the government's priorities going at the present time? We need to use some sense when discussing these points. When this type of development is encouraged, jobs will be created and there will be some economic activity-but this is really not the rationale. The question we must consider is whether it is the best type of development, whether it is the best use of the resources, whether it is the best investment and whether it is doing the best possible job for Canada. I suggest that the type of priorities the Liberal government will give to those industries in this legislation will not produce the best possible results for Canadians.
If I understand some statements correctly, there are people who would like to see an even better bill as it affects the mining and petroleum industries. Mr. Chairman, they have had certain concessions made to them as embodied in this legislation and in statements made from time to time by the Minister of Finance which extend the present situation until 1976. At the same time, there are suggestions that the tax system is stifling development in the basic resource industries in Canada. What more do they want? The only thing I can suggest is that they want the entire country. I am not prepared to see that happen.
When deciding on our tax policy and our development policy we will have to decide on certain priorities. We will have to decide if the structure of our tax system and development policy will be carried out in a way that will produce the best possible development for Canada. The Carter report which was tabled in 1966 came out in favour of the principle of tax neutrality; in other words, that the tax system should be structured in such a way as not to
November 23, 1971

encourage or favour one type of development against another. That is really a classic capitalistic approach to taxation, but obviously the government has rejected it, particularly with regard to the treatment of the mining and petroleum industries.
We must decide whether this is the best type of priority to give Canadian development and if it is the best way to serve the interests of the Canadian people. I have yet to hear a defence from the government to the effect that this is the best way to serve our interests.
We also need to look at the nature of the industries benefiting from some of the concessions allowed in this legislation. Most industries are foreign-owned; I think this is recognized and acknowledged. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Calgary North earlier this evening made reference to the fact that the petroleum industry is largely international in nature. That is known to all of us. What makes me rather sad is that people seem to be prepared to accept this type of structure and even further distortion of that structure. They are prepared to accept this international structure and the fact that people outside Canada will determine what is best for us and what sort of development will be carried out in this country.
This is what our national debate is about at the present time. Are we going to allow this situation to continue? Is this the type of Canada we want? I suggest that in the area of basic resource industries we must come to grips with the question. Recognizing what the situation is on an international scale, there are some things that Canada can do. Why is the Canadian government not setting up some form of consortium to deal with the entire complex of energy resources and the development of those resources from the production of the raw material to the finished products?
I think we have some of the necessary elements within the structure of government that would enable the government, through a properly established Canada Development Corporation, to take a lead in this field. Why is it not possible through Panarctic Oils, through Northern Transportation Company, through the Northern Power Commission and industrial complexes such as Polymer to set up an energy complex that could serve the industries of Canada and be a model for the world? It would put us in the forefront of industrial development.
There are other things we can do. We can work with the co-operative movement. It has a well established oil refinery in the city of Regina which is a source of pride to the people of my riding and to Saskatchewan. We have some oil activity by the co-operative movement in western Canada. There are many groups in many areas with whom the government could initiate and encourage effort in development. There are other groups which could take part in national development. I suggest that is the type of thing we should encourage if we are to see a rational development of resources in this country and change the direction of development so that it serves the interests of the Canadian people first, rather than the interests of foreign shareholders.
We must also recognize that some of the industries which benefit from these concessions create only a low level of employment; the ratio of employment to invest-
* Income Tax Act
ment is very low. This fact must be kept in mind when deciding our priorities in respect of development policy. It is clear that tax policies as embodied in Bill C-259 encouraged this type of development in Canada rather than other types of development which would be of greater benefit to the Canadian people. Therefore, there must be some change in emphasis.
We must bear in mind that the international companies to which I referred earlier operate only from self-interest. We have such companies in western Canada. Companies like Imperial Oil have carried on exploration and development activities in Alberta, Saskatchewan and, to a degree, in Manitoba. What happened with regard to these companies? They employed different crews for different jobs. They employed management people, office people, service people, and so on, in each of those provinces.
Then the companies decided to centralize their operations. First, they were going to centralize their operations in Edmonton or Calgary. Of course, certain people in western Canada said they were doing this because of the socialist government of Saskatchewan, or for any number of different reasons of that sort. Yet when the change of government took place in Saskatchewan in 1964, when a Liberal government took office and embraced the philosophy of private enterprise in all its forms, the exodus continued: the oil companies kept pulling out of Saskatchewan and moving their offices to Edmonton and Calgary.
That was because of the NDP government.

If my hon. friend had been listening he would have heard me say that this happened during the regime of the Liberal government in Saskatchewan. The hon. member should take note of what happened after the Liberal government took office. Apparently everything was fine; yet, some of these companies moved, as I say, to Edmonton and Calgary, the homeland of free, private enterprise. But what is happening now? In many cases they are moving from Edmonton and Calgary to Toronto. They are moving some of their facilities out of the west altogether. They are serving their own corporate interests first, second and last. It does not matter to them whether they are helping or hurting the areas from which they have taken their resources as long as they get their profit from the enterprise.
We see another example of this when we examine the actions of Imperial Oil in western Canada in centralizing its refining operation entirely in Edmonton and closing down operations in Calgary, Regina and Winnipeg. In each of the three prairie provinces refineries will be closed. That company does not think of the welfare and well-being of the community or province in which it enjoyed privileges and benefits over the years. It is thinking solely of its own corporate interest. I suggest that the day is long past when we can allow this sort of situation to continue.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard diverse views this evening on the type of consideration that should be given under the Canadian tax structure to developers of our resource industries. I was interested to hear the views of the hon. member for Regina East who tried to compare the benefits accruing to Canadians from the mining industry with the benefits accruing to them from co-operatives and credit unions.
Many members of the committee, myself included, spoke the other evening when the committee was considering the tax structure and proposals affecting co-operatives and credit unions. Those who spoke were justified in defending credit unions and co-operatives and in opposing the measures affecting those organizations which the government wishes to incorporate in this tax bill. I point out to the hon. member for Regina East that when he talks about people deriving benefits from credit unions and co-operatives he is referring to a great number of people, but the benefits which credit unions and co-operatives make available are comparatively small. On the other hand, he ought to take note of the fact that the mining industry of Canada employs directly about 150,000 people.
Of course, we must bear in mind that that is not the total extent of tht industry's impact on employment in Canada since for every employee in the mining industry there are seven or eight who work in other parts of Canada in industries associated with that industry. Their employment is assured because of the operation of our mines. So we are really talking about 150,000 people who are directly employed in the mining industry of Canada, and when we consider the over-all effect of that industry on the economy we are talking of approximately one million people employed in industries which depend directly on mining.
Before I deal further with how the tax structure affects the mining industry I should like to show briefly how some of the tax changes proposed by the government affect directly one of the most important elements of the Canadian mining industry's economy. I am talking about
[The Chairman.]
the person who is responsible for the establishment of mines in Canada, the original prospector. The Canadian mining industry is our most important industry, accounting for more than 40 per cent of our export dollars, with well over 25 Canadian communities being entirely dependent upon it.
It would be hard to conceive a Canadian economy without the financial contribution of mining companies such as Bay Mining and Smelting Company, International Nickel Company of Canada, Sherritt Gordon Mines, Consolidated Mining and Smelting, Noranda, Falconbridge, etc. In trying to assess the effects of the proposed tax changes upon this industry one may well start at the very beginning of it all, the prospector. Who among us, except the present government, would begrudge the original prospector and his courageous grubstakers the tax free earnings for which they may very seldom, if ever, qualify?
As has been mentioned during this debate, the prospector's work is arduous and demanding. Although the prospector can take full credit for the original discovery of all our operating mines, very seldom does he experience a big strike. It is a retrograde step to take incentive from the prospector. I suggest to the government that the prospector and his grubstakers need more incentive, not less.
It is safe to say that if it had not been for the prospector and the willingness of such concerns as the mining companies which I have mentioned, the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, Sherritt Gordon and International Nickel, to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in their findings, northern Manitoba would still be a sleeping wilderness. I might add that a substantial amount of the capital invested in this area was from foreign sources which some people in this House so roundly castigate.
The mining industry presents quite special characteristics and risks, many of which are unlike those encountered in other industries. Mining is concerned with a nonrenewable resource and the success or failure of mining operations depends entirely on the inherent unpredictability of ore bodies. Furthermore, the establishment of a producing mine frequently entails the complete build-up of new infrastructures, particularly in the more remote areas. Thompson, Manitoba, is a good example. In the year 1961 the population of Thompson was about 1,300. In 1963, just two years later, the population of this rapidly growing town had increased to approximately 7,000. The present population of Thompson is estimated at 23,000.
It is expected, justifiably, that the population will surpass 25,000 within the next few years. Here we see the development of an area which 11 years ago was nothing but forest, bush and rock. It is now one of the most modern cities in Canada. In a period of 11 years, the population has increased to 23,000. Can we imagine the number of families who have been dependent upon the mine for their livelihood?
I can also speak of the city of Flin Flon, Manitoba, where I have resided for a number of years. Tens of thousands of wage earners have raised their families in this town and have made it their home. They have found that it has a very fine atmosphere in which to raise a family. All this has come about through private investment and, to a large extent, foreign investment in Canada.
November 23, 1971

I am sure all members agree it would be a very fine situation if Canadians could come up with a system whereby most of our resource industries could be financed through Canadian investment. This government has come forward with a number of suggestions which have proven to be of no avail. No one has yet come up with the answer for which Canadians are looking. I am sure that everyone will agree that it would be a wonderful situation if we could arrive at that. However, we must face reality. If we are to have development in Canada, particularly of the resource industries, we must look for investment from wherever we can get it.
As the hon. member for Calgary South said, we hear a great deal of criticism from members of the NDP. They are continually saying that this is not the thing for Canadian industry. However, where do they go to get capital when it is necessary to float loans for the province of Manitoba, and I suppose, now, the province of Saskatchewan? The first place they go is across the border, the United States. This again proves that if the money that is needed is not available in Canada, we must face reality and turn to where it is available and people are ready and willing to invest in our country. As I said before, if we can come up with satisfactory measures whereby Canadian capital assumes far greater control over our industries, particularly our resource industries, we will all be very happy to see that day.
With regard to the development of our country, I am sure we all agree that if it had not been for private enterprise and initiative our resource industries would not have been developed. Canada would have been much more backward than it is today.

Hear, hear!
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, November 8, during the question period I addressed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) concerning the Old Age Security Act. In particular, I reminded the minister that during the debate on that act last December he made the statement several times that the basic amount of the pension was not necessarily frozen at $80 a month but could be increased by Parliament at any time. On the basis of that assertion, as recorded at page 9409, of Hansard, I put my question to the minister in these words:
-is the minister, in view of the needs of our pensioners, now considering an increase in that basic amount?
The reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare was at least clear and direct. It was in these words:
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
"Not at this time, Mr. Speaker." So I put to the minister a supplementary question in these terms:
Then is the minister considering the lowering of the eligible age for those who are prepared to retire from the labour market?
And the reply was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, as we indicated, I believe in our white paper on income security, we see this as a future trend. In terms of immediate action the government does not have any plans at this time.
My question was thus in two parts. On the one hand it asked for action to increase the basic amount of the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act, which at the moment is $80 a month; on the other hand, it asked for a new departure, namely, the lowering of the age at which a person might receive old age security benefits on the understanding that such a person would withdraw from the labour market.
I posted this two-part question for a "late show," Mr. Speaker, because it seemed to me that both parts of it are extremely important. Although we may not get finality by way of an answer in a "late show" period I believe this is one of the areas we ought to keep alive until we win. I assert as strongly as I can that the amount of the old age pension must not be left at $80. One of the reasons I feel pensions should be increased at this time is to offset a suggestion made in a report from the other place to the effect that old age security benefits might be wiped out and replaced by another program suggested in that report. It seems to me that the universal nature of old age security provisions is still one of the best things we have established in this Parliament and I believe the government should underwrite that good piece of legislation by increasing the amount, and that it should do so very soon.
The other part of the question is, I submit, of equal importance. The minister referred to future trends. The day will come when retirement at an earlier age will be a fact in our society. In light of today's unemployment among young people I believe we should start that day now. I suggest, therefore, as clearly as I can, that both old age security and benefits under the Canada Pension Plan should be made available at age 60 to those who are prepared to withdraw from the labour market. This is a test which we apply in certain other instances. In other words, other income which people receive should not interfere with getting these pensions earlier. I suggest it makes sound common sense to establish the principle that people who are prepared to withdraw from the labour market at 60 should get both their old age security benefits and their Canada Pension Plan payments, for both of which individual Canadians are now paying under our tax laws and under the terms of the Canada Pension Plan.
So I present these two ideas in the form of this two-part question again tonight, hoping there will be some ray of hope forthcoming from the government side-that the day will soon come when the amount of the old age security pension will be increased and when the eligible age will be lowered at least on the terms I have suggested.

maintopic: RKGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-RE-EVALUATION OF POLICIES IN LIGHT OF CRITICISMS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 22 I directed a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) in respect of a statement reported in the press to have been made by the Prime Minister of Quebec to the effect that the government's regional economic expansion policies were having no effect in that province.
The answer I received from the minister was that he had checked with the Prime Minister of Quebec that very day and he had denied having made such a statement. My question was prompted by a story which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Friday, November 19. I quote from it as follows:
Noting that Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau had campaigned on the platform of combating regional inequalities, the premier said: "Regional disparities . . . have not yet been affected by federal policies after 31 years of power."	[DOT]
The question originally arose from a story which came from the Quebec City bureau of Canadian Press. It was a consequence of a story which appeared in the French newspaper Le Soleil, a Quebec City daily. There is no question in my mind that the government of Quebec is unhappy with the policies of this government in respect of regional development, or that this story was carried by Canadian Press in the Globe and Mail, in the Saturday edition of the Montreal Gazette and the Quebec City daily Le Soleil.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Premier made such a statement, because I have checked my sources and the story is on electronic tape and was covered by Canadian Press and Le Soleil. My question was not directly as a result of what the Premier of Quebec is reported to have said, although it would be warranted on the basis of that fact alone. This is merely another of a series of criticisms levelled at this government's regional economic expansion policies.
The Prime Minister of Quebec was merely echoing statements which had been made by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council at a general meeting in the city of Fredericton last October and levelled similar criticisms at the regional economic expansion policies of the government. The first report of the Atlantic Development Council stated, in effect, that the government was lacking an effective strategy on regional development for the Atlantic provinces.
This, I might add, is one of the agencies charged by statute with advising the minister on regional economic policies for the Atlantic provinces. There were also reports by the Canadian Council of Rural Development, which is another agency charged by law with advising the minister on regional economic policies. In addition, there was evidence presented to the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion.
All this evidence indicates that there is general dissatisfaction in the country, not with the principle of regional economic expansion but with the way in which this government is going about it. The policy is overly centralized; it lacks an over-all strategy and does not pay any regard to regional peculiarities or regional differences. For example, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council in its fifth annual report suggested that the department was overly centralized and that there should be, in fact, an assistant deputy minister and staff stationed in the Atlantic provinces to pay attention to the peculiar interests of the Atlantic provinces.
But overriding all these criticisms is the fact that regional development policies within the government's framework are ineffective because government fiscal and monetary policies render them ineffective and they are at cross-purposes with one another. Consequently, today we have a situation developing in this country where there is unanimous disapproval of the policies of the government in attempting to combat regional disparities. This, I believe, is the main problem facing this country.
The program established by the government is overly centralized and does not pay any attention to the advice of the agencies which are charged by statute with the responsibility of rendering advice to the government. The department does not consult regional bodies or municipalities. In my view it does not consult the provinces in conceiving and executing its policies. The result is we have substantial sums from the federal budget going into a program to combat regional disparities which is not very effective.
When we consider that the Prime Minister of Quebec did make the charge-his comments are on record with Canadian Press and Le Soleil on electronic tape-that the policies of the government in the last 3 J years have had no

November 23, 1971

effect in the province of Quebec, and that over 50 per cent of federal funds allocated by Parliament for regional development has gone into that province, we have some idea of the seriousness of these charges. That is what prompted my question.

I welcome the remarks of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), particularly that part which, as he said at the beginning, was essentially intended to be constructive. He raised two questions. The first is the question as to what in fact the premier of Quebec did say.
There appears to be a certain conflict between the newspaper evidence which he cited and what the minister reported the Premier of Quebec said. I suggest, however, that that is not the important question. Upon occasion journalists make slips of the pen and on occasion politicians make slips of the tongue. I myself have even been known on occasion to make a slip of the tongue. But really the issue is not what the Premier said but whether in fact the programs are working effectively in the province of Quebec and in the Maritimes.
I submit that if one visits Quebec and sees some of the work that has been done under the programs of the department, one can see that there has been a successful resolution to many of the efforts of the department. I would say that that is true also in the Atlantic provinces, although in my new position I have not yet had the opportunity to visit that area. However, I hope to visit it tomorrow if it becomes sufficiently free from fog so that the plane can land.

There have been criticisms of the department and we welcome them. It gives us a chance to reassess the program which is now in its third year. As the minister has often said, the time spent on this program in terms of successful efforts can only be judged over a 15-year period. No one has ever contended that the efforts of the department will solve problems overnight, like a magic wand, or even in the space of two or three years resolve the problems of regional disparity which have faced this country for over a century. But I am convinced that the various reports which we have received from the Atlantic Development Council and from APEC have been helpful.
We certainly do not agree with all the criticisms levelled against the government. Nor, I would suggest, have these bodies, as the hon. member contends, always unanimously opposed the government's program. For instance, interesting statements have been made in support of the program by representatives of the city of St. John's at the APEC conference. There has been some support and some opposition to what the department is doing. We hope to take into account those criticisms which are constructive, which will enable us to improve programs which we

offer, and to continue what has already proved successful in the area of regional development.

HEALTH-FAMILY PLANNING CONFERENCE-REQUEST FOR PUBLICITY CAMPAIGNS BECAUSE OF INCREASE IN ILLEGITIMATE BIRTHS
speechtext:
As I
indicated the other day, I welcome the minister's announcement that a National Family Planning Conference is to be held in February of next year. Also, I was glad to hear his answer to my question asking which organizations would be invited to participate. I understand that just about every organization of a voluntary nature, in the private area, of which we are aware has in the past shown interest in this subject. The Minister's speech in Halifax last Friday to the annual meeting of the Family Planning Federation of Canada gives further hope of government action, promising as it did to ask Parliament, probably next month, for additional manpower and money for family planning purposes. It is indeed welcome news.
However, I am pursuing the matter further tonight because I am deeply concerned about the need for swift and far reaching action in the matter of family planning. Figures issued by the minister's department last September are a frightening forecast of the future we can expect if we fail to initiate vigorous action without delay. In the 20 years before 1959 the illegitimate birth rate in Canada fluctuated between 3.8 per cent and 4 per cent of live births, except for the war years when it rose fractionally. But in 1959 it started a steady climb year by year until it reached 9.2 per cent of live births in 1969. Almost one-tenth of Canadian babies born in 1969 were illegitimate. To whom were they born? More then three-quarters of them were born to girls and women between the ages of 15 and 24.
One thinks of the effect on these mothers, many of them teenagers. One thinks of the effect on these unwanted babies, some handed over to institutions, some battered in common law marriages, some developing into delinquents and criminals and, of course, some finding good foster homes. One thinks of the cost to the community, not only in taxes but in the tragic lowering of security and citizenship standards. One thinks of all these things and agrees with the sober words of the report that this illegitimacy figure "indicates the great need for an educational program in family planning that would begin at the elementary school level."
Who is to initiate such a program? Obviously its implementation will require the co-operation of all levels of government as well as voluntary associations. But the responsibility for initiating the program is clearly that of the federal government. The report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women has a number of excellent recommendations, including the one "that birth control information be available to everyone." Further, it recommends that "the Department of National Health and Welfare (a) prepare and offer birth control information free of charge to provincial and territorial authorities, associations, organizations and individuals and (b) give financial

November 23, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
assistance through national health grants and national welfare grants to train health and welfare workers in family planning techniques."
As far as I am aware the department has thus far given financial assistance to only two family planning organizations, in the total amount of $125,000. Such an amount is only a start. Of course, it will be costly to bring birth control information and help to the people of Canada. We are getting a late start. After all, birth control was a criminal offence in this country between 1892 and 1969- three-quarters of a fast changing century. We must make up for a lot of lost time.
A government that could find $9 million to finance the B and B Commission and nearly $3 i million to finance the Prices and Incomes Commission could surely manage to find comparable revenues to help women avoid compulsory pregnancy, to prevent the arrival in the world of unwanted babies and to cut down the great numbers of abortions, legal and illegal, that will continue to swell until people get the information and the contraceptives that will enable them to plan, space and limit their families.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the third time in a few weeks the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has brought up family planning. We know her deep concern with that issue. However, it seems quite strange to us that the hon. member should seem unaware of the activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare in that field, since she is constantly bringing up the matter. The government has a family planning program which has been described many times right here in the House.
The conference to which the hon. member referred in her question of November 17 is to group close to 250 delegates here in Ottawa next February. These delegates will be representing provincial groups, health and welfare groups, volunteer organizations and citizens' groups, all dedicated to the cause of family planning. This national conference-the first of its kind-will afford an excellent
opportunity for delegates to exchange their experiences. Among other things, the conference will deal with the training of personnel in that field, the needs for research as well as information. It will review the various existing programs so as to better direct the development of future programs.
On November 19, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) made an important speech at the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Family Planning, in Halifax. He said, among other things, that this conference would be an excellent opportunity for participants to consider the place that family planning should occupy in a broader context of training for family life. The report that the Vanier Institute of the Family published in April 1971 indicated that only 31 per cent of schools being surveyed proposed some kind of training for family life. However, a survey made by the Canadian Press and published in October 1971 points to constant progress in this field over the past three or four years. The method and content vary considerably from one school to the next; courses, seldom compulsory, are often optional or extra-curricular. The subject is generally part of a course on hygiene, integrated into lessons on domestic orientation. They give outlines of the biology of reproduction and a complete course on the growth and maturation process, family relationships and responsibilities, and tensions which are felt inside the family and the community. According to the report by the Vanier Institute of the Family, educators are mainly concerned with training teachers and inserting free time periods in the programs. This raises the question of the responsibility for the education for family life in our schools, and that of the practice of this education.
School boards, conscious of the importance of this matter, develop at an ever increasing rate these programs which are now part of the curriculum. It is to be hoped that these programs of training for family life will become more and more popular and constitute at least a partial solution to the tragic problem of illegitimate births.
